questions.prompt: How many principles does the PMBOK Guide 8th Edition define?
questions.rationale: PMBOK 8 condenses the 12 principles of the 7th edition into 6 action-guiding statements.

option_rationales.a: 12 was the count in PMBOK 7, not the 8th edition.
option_rationales.b: 8 is the number of PMBOK 7 performance domains, not principles.
option_rationales.c: PMBOK 8 condenses the 12 principles of the 7th edition into 6 action-guiding statements.
option_rationales.d: No edition of the guide defines five principles.

questions.prompt: What share of the 2026 PMP exam is the Business Environment domain?
questions.rationale: Business Environment rises from 8% to 26% — the biggest single change in the 2026 ECO.

option_rationales.a: 8% was the weighting in the previous ECO, before the 2026 update.
option_rationales.b: 16% does not correspond to any 2026 domain weighting.
option_rationales.c: Business Environment rises from 8% to 26% — the biggest single change in the 2026 ECO.
option_rationales.d: 41% is the weighting of the Process domain.

questions.prompt: Where are the cross-cutting themes (principles, AI, sustainability, value) tested?

options.text: Across all three domains, blended into scenario questions
Only in the Business Environment domain
Only in a dedicated section at the start of the exam
They are background reading and are not examined

questions.rationale: The cross-cutting themes are not a separate domain; they surface in People, Process and Business Environment alike.

option_rationales.a: The cross-cutting themes are not a separate domain; they surface in People, Process and Business Environment alike.
option_rationales.b: They are anchored in Business Environment but examined everywhere.
option_rationales.c: The exam contains no separate cross-cutting section.
option_rationales.d: They are explicitly examinable content in 2026, not background reading.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the six PMBOK 8 principles?

options.text: Adopt a Holistic View
Navigate Complexity
Integrate Sustainability
Build an Empowered Culture

questions.rationale: 'Navigate Complexity' was a PMBOK 7 principle; it is absorbed into 'Adopt a Holistic View' in PMBOK 8.

option_rationales.a: Adopt a Holistic View is one of the six.
option_rationales.b: 'Navigate Complexity' was a PMBOK 7 principle; it is absorbed into 'Adopt a Holistic View' in PMBOK 8.
option_rationales.c: Integrate Sustainability is one of the six — indeed the new one.
option_rationales.d: Build an Empowered Culture is one of the six.

questions.prompt: Which principle is genuinely new as a standalone principle in PMBOK 8?

options.text: Focus on Value
Embed Quality into Processes and Deliverables
Integrate Sustainability
Be an Accountable Leader

questions.rationale: Integrate Sustainability is the new standalone principle, reflecting the rising weight of ESG in the 2026 exam.

option_rationales.a: Focus on Value already existed in PMBOK 7.
option_rationales.b: Quality was already a principle in PMBOK 7.
option_rationales.c: Integrate Sustainability is the new standalone principle, reflecting the rising weight of ESG in the 2026 exam.
option_rationales.d: Leadership and stewardship existed before; they were merged, not created.

questions.prompt: A project manager realises that a timetable change will affect connecting services, crew rosters and customers, and maps those interactions before deciding. Which principle is being applied?

options.text: Build an Empowered Culture
Focus on Value
Embed Quality
Adopt a Holistic View

questions.rationale: Seeing the project as a system in its environment, with interactions and context, is Adopt a Holistic View.

option_rationales.a: Nothing is said about enabling the team.
option_rationales.b: No value trade-off is described; the point is the web of interactions.
option_rationales.c: No quality practice appears in the scenario.
option_rationales.d: Seeing the project as a system in its environment, with interactions and context, is Adopt a Holistic View.

questions.prompt: A team is about to build a feature that no user has asked for and that no metric tracks. Which principle most directly argues against building it?

options.text: Focus on Value
Embed Quality
Be an Accountable Leader
Integrate Sustainability

questions.rationale: Focus on Value steers decisions by benefit created rather than by completing tasks; unused output is wasted capacity.

option_rationales.a: Focus on Value steers decisions by benefit created rather than by completing tasks; unused output is wasted capacity.
option_rationales.b: Quality is not the issue — the feature could be built perfectly.
option_rationales.c: Nobody's accountability is in question here.
option_rationales.d: No environmental or social impact is described.

questions.prompt: A team agrees a Definition of Done and runs peer reviews during each iteration rather than relying on a final inspection. Which principle does this express?

options.text: Focus on Value
Embed Quality into Processes and Deliverables
Adopt a Holistic View
Build an Empowered Culture

questions.rationale: Embedding quality means building it into processes and deliverables, preventing defects early instead of inspecting at the end.

option_rationales.a: A value focus alone does not require reviews or a Definition of Done.
option_rationales.b: Embedding quality means building it into processes and deliverables, preventing defects early instead of inspecting at the end.
option_rationales.c: No system-level interactions are described.
option_rationales.d: The example concerns quality practice, not team empowerment.

questions.prompt: A project manager has no line authority over the team but still takes responsibility for outcomes, is transparent about problems and models the behaviour they expect. Which principle is this?

options.text: Focus on Value
Build an Empowered Culture
Be an Accountable Leader
Integrate Sustainability

questions.rationale: Be an Accountable Leader means taking responsibility and leading by example regardless of formal authority.

option_rationales.a: No value trade-off appears in the scenario.
option_rationales.b: Nothing is said about enabling the team to act.
option_rationales.c: Be an Accountable Leader means taking responsibility and leading by example regardless of formal authority.
option_rationales.d: No sustainability aspect is described.

questions.prompt: A project manager deliberately creates an environment where the team makes its own technical decisions and stakeholders are actively engaged. Which principle is this?

options.text: Be an Accountable Leader
Adopt a Holistic View
Embed Quality
Build an Empowered Culture

questions.rationale: Build an Empowered Culture bundles the PMBOK 7 team and stakeholder principles into enabling people to be effective.

option_rationales.a: Accountability is not what is described; the focus is enabling others.
option_rationales.b: No system-level interactions are described.
option_rationales.c: No quality practice appears here.
option_rationales.d: Build an Empowered Culture bundles the PMBOK 7 team and stakeholder principles into enabling people to be effective.

questions.prompt: How should the six principles be used in an exam scenario?

options.text: As a decision lens for judging which behaviour is appropriate
As rules to be recited verbatim
As a checklist that must be fully completed on every project
As optional guidance that applies only to agile projects

questions.rationale: Principles are not memorisation items; the exam asks which behaviour is right in a given scenario.

option_rationales.a: Principles are not memorisation items; the exam asks which behaviour is right in a given scenario.
option_rationales.b: Principles are not memorisation items.
option_rationales.c: Principles are not a checklist to be completed.
option_rationales.d: They apply to every delivery approach, not only agile.

questions.prompt: A sponsor demands maximum speed. The project manager presents three options with their cost, risk and sustainability consequences and lets the sponsor decide. Which principle is best demonstrated?

options.text: Focus on Value
Be an Accountable Leader
Embed Quality
Integrate Sustainability

questions.rationale: Showing options and consequences transparently, rather than silently complying, is accountable leadership.

option_rationales.a: The value question is not what this behaviour demonstrates.
option_rationales.b: Showing options and consequences transparently, rather than silently complying, is accountable leadership.
option_rationales.c: No quality practice is involved.
option_rationales.d: Sustainability is only one of several consequences being shown.

questions.prompt: A cheaper, non-recycled supplier would meet the deadline comfortably; the recycled option only just meets it. Which two principles are most clearly in tension?

options.text: Embed Quality and Adopt a Holistic View
Be an Accountable Leader and Embed Quality
Focus on Value and Integrate Sustainability
Build an Empowered Culture and Focus on Value

questions.rationale: Value read narrowly as cost pulls one way; sustainability pulls the other — the exam expects a justified trade-off.

option_rationales.a: Quality and holistic thinking are not the poles of this trade-off.
option_rationales.b: Accountability is how you handle the trade-off, not the trade-off itself.
option_rationales.c: Value read narrowly as cost pulls one way; sustainability pulls the other — the exam expects a justified trade-off.
option_rationales.d: Team empowerment plays no part in the supplier decision.

questions.prompt: The PMBOK 7 principles 'Stewardship' and 'Leadership' are mainly condensed into which PMBOK 8 principle?

options.text: Build an Empowered Culture
Adopt a Holistic View
Focus on Value
Be an Accountable Leader

questions.rationale: Stewardship and leadership are combined into Be an Accountable Leader.

option_rationales.a: Empowered Culture absorbs the team and stakeholder principles.
option_rationales.b: Holistic View absorbs systems thinking, complexity and tailoring.
option_rationales.c: Focus on Value absorbs value and change toward the target state.
option_rationales.d: Stewardship and leadership are combined into Be an Accountable Leader.

questions.prompt: Under 'Focus on Value', how should value be interpreted?

options.text: As benefit in the broadest sense, including accessibility, reputation and long-term operating cost
As schedule performance against the baseline
Strictly as monetary return
As the number of deliverables produced

questions.rationale: Value is broader than money; it includes societal, reputational and life-cycle benefits.

option_rationales.a: Value is broader than money; it includes societal, reputational and life-cycle benefits.
option_rationales.b: Schedule adherence is a constraint, not value.
option_rationales.c: Money is only one part of value.
option_rationales.d: Output volume says nothing about the value created.

questions.prompt: Where did the PMBOK 7 principles on risk and adaptability go in PMBOK 8?

options.text: They were removed from the framework entirely
They were absorbed into Adopt a Holistic View and the performance domains
They became two of the five focus areas
They were merged into Integrate Sustainability

questions.rationale: Risk and adaptability did not disappear; they moved into holistic thinking and the domains.

option_rationales.a: They were redistributed, not deleted.
option_rationales.b: Risk and adaptability did not disappear; they moved into holistic thinking and the domains.
option_rationales.c: The focus areas are Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling and Closing.
option_rationales.d: Sustainability is a distinct new principle, unrelated to this.

questions.prompt: An AI tool drafts the weekly status report automatically. Under responsible AI use, this is:

options.text: Unacceptable — reporting must always be written by hand
Acceptable only if the sponsor is unaware it was AI-generated
Acceptable, provided the project manager reviews and releases it before distribution
Acceptable only for internal audiences, never for the sponsor

questions.rationale: AI for drafting is fine when human control and release remain with the project manager.

option_rationales.a: Manual writing is not required; supervised AI drafting is acceptable.
option_rationales.b: Concealing AI use breaches transparency.
option_rationales.c: AI for drafting is fine when human control and release remain with the project manager.
option_rationales.d: The audience is irrelevant — review before sending is what matters.

questions.prompt: A project manager pastes a confidential supplier bid into a public web AI tool to summarise it. What is the primary problem?

options.text: The summary may be too short
AI cannot summarise commercial documents
It is slower than reading the bid
It breaches confidentiality and data-protection obligations

questions.rationale: Sensitive data must not go into open systems; this is a governance and compliance failure.

option_rationales.a: Length is not the problem.
option_rationales.b: AI can summarise it — which is precisely the problem here.
option_rationales.c: Speed is irrelevant beside the confidentiality breach.
option_rationales.d: Sensitive data must not go into open systems; this is a governance and compliance failure.

questions.prompt: An AI tool reorders the product backlog and the project manager adopts the order without review. What is wrong?

options.text: Accountability is bypassed; prioritisation remains a human decision with a rationale
Backlogs may never be prioritised with tool support
Nothing — the tool has more data than the team
The tool should have been asked to explain itself in writing

questions.rationale: AI output is an input; the PM or Product Owner still owns and justifies prioritisation.

option_rationales.a: AI output is an input; the PM or Product Owner still owns and justifies prioritisation.
option_rationales.b: Tool support for prioritisation is entirely legitimate.
option_rationales.c: More data does not transfer accountability to a tool.
option_rationales.d: An explanation does not restore human ownership of the decision.

questions.prompt: An AI estimate is 20% shorter than the team's bottom-up estimate, but the tool was trained on data from regions with faster approvals. What should the project manager do FIRST?

options.text: Commit to the earlier date to satisfy the sponsor
Validate the data basis and compare against the team estimate and historical approval times
Discard the AI estimate as unusable
Ask the team to re-estimate until they match the tool

questions.rationale: Transferability of the training data is the decisive check before any commitment.

option_rationales.a: Committing before validation is exactly the trap being tested.
option_rationales.b: Transferability of the training data is the decisive check before any commitment.
option_rationales.c: The forecast becomes usable once its data basis is checked.
option_rationales.d: Forcing estimates to match a tool destroys the independent check.

questions.prompt: An AI-generated cost forecast proves badly wrong. Who is accountable?

options.text: The project manager
The tool vendor
The data science team
Nobody — AI errors are unforeseeable

questions.rationale: Accountability stays with the project manager; the tool is not a decision-maker.

option_rationales.a: Accountability stays with the project manager; the tool is not a decision-maker.
option_rationales.b: Vendors supply tools, not project accountability.
option_rationales.c: Data specialists support; they do not carry project accountability.
option_rationales.d: Accountability never disappears.

questions.prompt: What is an AI 'hallucination' in a project context?

options.text: A deliberate falsification by a team member
A forecast that is correct but arrives too late
A delay caused by tool downtime
An output that looks plausible and confident but is factually wrong

questions.rationale: Hallucinations are convincing but incorrect outputs — the reason validation is mandatory.

option_rationales.a: Hallucination is a model behaviour, not human misconduct.
option_rationales.b: Timeliness is a separate problem.
option_rationales.c: Downtime is an availability issue, not a hallucination.
option_rationales.d: Hallucinations are convincing but incorrect outputs — the reason validation is mandatory.

questions.prompt: AI flags a schedule risk early; the project manager verifies it and escalates. This is best described as:

options.text: Exemplary use — AI as early warning, human validation and action
A compliance breach
Over-reliance on automation
Unnecessary duplication of effort

questions.rationale: Early warning plus human validation is the model pattern for responsible AI use.

option_rationales.a: Early warning plus human validation is the model pattern for responsible AI use.
option_rationales.b: Nothing here breaches a rule or policy.
option_rationales.c: Over-reliance would mean acting without verification — the opposite happened.
option_rationales.d: Verification is control, not duplicated effort.

questions.prompt: Regarding transparency, what should a project manager do about AI use?

options.text: Keep it confidential to avoid undermining confidence
Disclose it to the team and sponsor and have results validated
Disclose it only if asked directly
Disclose it only when the output turns out to be wrong

questions.rationale: Transparency about AI use, plus validation, is part of accountable practice.

option_rationales.a: Concealment undermines trust rather than protecting it.
option_rationales.b: Transparency about AI use, plus validation, is part of accountable practice.
option_rationales.c: Waiting to be asked is not transparency.
option_rationales.d: Disclosure only after failure comes too late.

questions.prompt: Why can biased or outdated training data be dangerous for AI forecasts?

options.text: It slows the tool down
It makes the tool refuse to answer
It produces confident forecasts that do not fit the current context
It automatically breaches data protection

questions.rationale: Patterns from unrepresentative data yield plausible but inapplicable predictions.

option_rationales.a: Bias affects output quality, not processing speed.
option_rationales.b: Biased models still answer — and confidently so.
option_rationales.c: Patterns from unrepresentative data yield plausible but inapplicable predictions.
option_rationales.d: Bias and data protection are separate issues.

questions.prompt: Where does AI typically deliver the most value in project management?

options.text: Making final go/no-go decisions
Replacing stakeholder relationships
Signing off contractual commitments
Data-intensive and routine work such as reporting, forecasting and pattern detection

questions.rationale: AI excels at data-heavy, repetitive analysis; judgement and accountability stay human.

option_rationales.a: Final decisions remain with people.
option_rationales.b: AI supports communication; it does not replace relationships.
option_rationales.c: Contractual commitment requires human authority.
option_rationales.d: AI excels at data-heavy, repetitive analysis; judgement and accountability stay human.

questions.prompt: A sponsor is delighted by an AI-generated earlier finish date and wants to announce it today. The BEST response is to:

options.text: Explain the validation still needed and offer a justified, possibly staged, statement
Refuse to discuss AI-generated dates at all
Announce it, since the tool is more objective than people
Delegate the decision to the team

questions.rationale: Accountable leadership means explaining what must be checked before a commitment is made.

option_rationales.a: Accountable leadership means explaining what must be checked before a commitment is made.
option_rationales.b: Refusing to engage is not accountable leadership.
option_rationales.c: A tool's apparent objectivity does not remove the need to validate.
option_rationales.d: The commitment decision is not the team's to make.

questions.prompt: 'Human in the loop' in project AI use means:

options.text: A person must physically operate the tool
A person reviews, validates and remains accountable for AI-supported outputs
AI may only be used in workshops with the team present
Every AI output must be recreated manually

questions.rationale: The principle is human review and retained accountability, not manual duplication.

option_rationales.a: It refers to oversight, not to physically operating the tool.
option_rationales.b: The principle is human review and retained accountability, not manual duplication.
option_rationales.c: It applies to every use, not only to workshops.
option_rationales.d: Recreating output manually defeats the purpose of using AI.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the exam's stance on AI in project management?

options.text: AI decisions are more reliable than human ones and should be followed
AI is prohibited in regulated environments
AI supports; the human checks, decides and is accountable
AI may only be used after project closure

questions.rationale: The recurring exam pattern is validate rather than blindly adopt.

option_rationales.a: Reliability depends on data and context; accountability stays human.
option_rationales.b: AI is not prohibited — it is governed.
option_rationales.c: The recurring exam pattern is validate rather than blindly adopt.
option_rationales.d: AI adds most value during the project, not after closure.

questions.prompt: Step-free access and noise protection for residents belong to which ESG pillar?

options.text: Social
Environmental
Governance
None — they are pure scope items

questions.rationale: Impact on people, safety and accessibility sits in the Social pillar.

option_rationales.a: Impact on people, safety and accessibility sits in the Social pillar.
option_rationales.b: Emissions and resource use would be Environmental.
option_rationales.c: Governance covers ethics and compliance, not impact on users.
option_rationales.d: Accessibility is a genuine ESG aspect, not merely a scope item.

questions.prompt: Using recycled ballast with a lower CO2 footprint is primarily which ESG pillar?

options.text: Environmental
Social
Governance
Economic only

questions.rationale: Resource use, emissions and life-cycle impact are Environmental.

option_rationales.a: Resource use, emissions and life-cycle impact are Environmental.
option_rationales.b: Social covers people, safety and accessibility.
option_rationales.c: Governance covers ethics, compliance and transparency.
option_rationales.d: Economics is not a separate ESG pillar.

questions.prompt: Transparent procurement, anti-corruption rules and origin records belong to:

options.text: Environmental
Governance
Social
Quality management only

questions.rationale: Ethics, compliance and transparency form the Governance pillar.

option_rationales.a: Environmental covers emissions and resource use.
option_rationales.b: Ethics, compliance and transparency form the Governance pillar.
option_rationales.c: Social covers people and community impact.
option_rationales.d: Quality management is a separate discipline.

questions.prompt: The 'triple bottom line' refers to:

options.text: Scope, schedule and cost
Plan, do and check
People, planet and profit
Prevention, appraisal and failure

questions.rationale: Sustainable projects optimise People, Planet and Profit together, not cost alone.

option_rationales.a: That is the classic triple constraint.
option_rationales.b: Plan-do-check is a quality improvement cycle.
option_rationales.c: Sustainable projects optimise People, Planet and Profit together, not cost alone.
option_rationales.d: Those are cost-of-quality categories.

questions.prompt: At which point is sustainability MOST effectively embedded?

options.text: During final acceptance testing
After handover, by the operations team
In the closing phase, as a lessons-learned item
In the business case and design, early in the life cycle

questions.rationale: Embedding sustainability early is cheapest and most effective; late changes are expensive.

option_rationales.a: By testing, the design is fixed and change has become expensive.
option_rationales.b: Operations inherit whatever the project already decided.
option_rationales.c: Lessons learned come far too late to influence the design.
option_rationales.d: Embedding sustainability early is cheapest and most effective; late changes are expensive.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a properly formulated sustainability metric?

options.text: 'CO2 per tonne of ballast reduced by 30% versus bidder A, measured at delivery'
'Sustainability will be considered throughout'
'We will be as green as possible'
'The supplier is certified'

questions.rationale: A usable metric has a baseline, a target value and a measurement point.

option_rationales.a: A usable metric has a baseline, a target value and a measurement point.
option_rationales.b: An intention, not a measurable value.
option_rationales.c: No target and no measurement — this is not a metric.
option_rationales.d: A certificate is evidence, not a project metric.

questions.prompt: A steering committee asks why it should pay 12% more for the sustainable bidder. The BEST justification is:

options.text: Sustainability is company policy, so there is no choice
The premium is offset by avoided emission costs, reputation, funding eligibility and lower operating risk
The cheaper bidder is technically unsuitable
The team prefers working with that supplier

questions.rationale: Sustainability convinces when expressed as total value, not as an attitude.

option_rationales.a: Policy compliance is weak justification before a steering committee.
option_rationales.b: Sustainability convinces when expressed as total value, not as an attitude.
option_rationales.c: Suitability is not the issue; the cheaper bid is technically compliant.
option_rationales.d: Team preference is not a business argument.

questions.prompt: Recycled material may vary in quality. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reject recycled material on principle
Accept the variance as unavoidable
Add the risk to the register with inspection and acceptance criteria
Transfer the entire risk to the operations team

questions.rationale: Sustainability choices create their own risks, which are managed actively rather than ignored.

option_rationales.a: Rejecting on principle discards the sustainability benefit entirely.
option_rationales.b: Accepting an unmanaged quality risk is not risk management.
option_rationales.c: Sustainability choices create their own risks, which are managed actively rather than ignored.
option_rationales.d: Transferring a project risk to operations does not manage it.

questions.prompt: The 'Integrate Sustainability' principle asks the project manager to consider impact:

options.text: Only during the project's execution phase
Only where legally mandated
Only for externally funded projects
Ecological, social and economic, extending beyond the project life cycle

questions.rationale: The principle explicitly reaches beyond project closure into operation and decommissioning.

option_rationales.a: The principle explicitly reaches beyond the project life cycle.
option_rationales.b: It applies regardless of the legal minimum.
option_rationales.c: It is not limited to a particular funding type.
option_rationales.d: The principle explicitly reaches beyond project closure into operation and decommissioning.

questions.prompt: Which entry point makes ESG binding on suppliers?

options.text: Including ESG criteria in procurement and contracts
Mentioning it in the kickoff presentation
Discussing it at the retrospective
Adding it to the lessons-learned register

questions.rationale: Contractual ESG criteria (supplier standards, origin, disposal) make sustainability enforceable.

option_rationales.a: Contractual ESG criteria (supplier standards, origin, disposal) make sustainability enforceable.
option_rationales.b: A mention at kickoff creates no obligation.
option_rationales.c: Retrospectives improve the team, not supplier duties.
option_rationales.d: The register captures learning, not contractual obligations.

questions.prompt: Which statement about sustainability trade-offs is correct?

options.text: Trade-offs should be resolved quietly by the project manager
Trade-offs should be made transparent so decision-makers can weigh cost against long-term value
Sustainability always outranks cost, so no trade-off exists
Trade-offs are a governance matter and not the project manager's concern

questions.rationale: Transparency about cost versus long-term value is what makes the decision defensible.

option_rationales.a: Silent resolution takes the decision away from those accountable for it.
option_rationales.b: Transparency about cost versus long-term value is what makes the decision defensible.
option_rationales.c: A blanket rule ignores context, cost and proportionality.
option_rationales.d: The project manager prepares and presents the trade-off.

questions.prompt: Put the value chain in the correct order.

options.text: Value → benefit → outcome → output
Outcome → output → value → benefit
Output → outcome → benefit → value
Benefit → output → outcome → value

questions.rationale: A deliverable (output) enables a change (outcome), which produces benefit and ultimately value.

option_rationales.a: This reverses the chain.
option_rationales.b: Output must precede outcome.
option_rationales.c: A deliverable (output) enables a change (outcome), which produces benefit and ultimately value.
option_rationales.d: Benefit cannot precede the output that enables it.

questions.prompt: An app is delivered on time and on budget, but only 8% of customers use it and the expected savings never appear. How should this be judged?

options.text: Not successful in value terms — output was delivered but benefit was not realised
Successful, because adoption is not the project's responsibility
Successful — the triple constraint was met
Impossible to judge until the next audit

questions.rationale: On time and on budget is necessary but not sufficient; success means realised benefit.

option_rationales.a: On time and on budget is necessary but not sufficient; success means realised benefit.
option_rationales.b: Planning adoption is part of delivering value.
option_rationales.c: Meeting the constraints is necessary but not sufficient.
option_rationales.d: The evidence is already available: adoption and savings both failed.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a LEADING indicator for a new booking app?

options.text: Weekly active users and booking-flow completion rate
Counter costs saved in euros
Annual ROI
Year-end customer satisfaction survey

questions.rationale: Leading indicators are early signals such as usage and adoption that allow you to steer in time.

option_rationales.a: Leading indicators are early signals such as usage and adoption that allow you to steer in time.
option_rationales.b: Cost savings materialise late.
option_rationales.c: ROI is a late, lagging result.
option_rationales.d: An annual survey is a lagging measure.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a LAGGING indicator?

options.text: App-store rating in week one
Return on investment after twelve months
Daily active users
Number of onboarding sessions held

questions.rationale: Lagging indicators are late results such as ROI, savings and satisfaction.

option_rationales.a: An early rating is a leading signal.
option_rationales.b: Lagging indicators are late results such as ROI, savings and satisfaction.
option_rationales.c: Daily usage is an early signal.
option_rationales.d: Activity counts measure effort, not results.

questions.prompt: Who should be accountable for benefit realisation after the project team disbands?

options.text: A named benefit owner, typically in product management or operations
The former project manager, indefinitely
The project sponsor's assistant
Nobody — benefits are realised automatically

questions.rationale: Value is realised in use, so a named owner beyond the project must measure and steer it.

option_rationales.a: Value is realised in use, so a named owner beyond the project must measure and steer it.
option_rationales.b: Indefinite ownership by a disbanded project manager is unrealistic.
option_rationales.c: Accountability must sit with a role that can actually act.
option_rationales.d: Benefits do not materialise without ownership.

questions.prompt: Which sequence describes benefits realisation?

options.text: Identify → deliver → disband → forget
Plan → deliver → close → archive
Deliver → measure → invoice → report
Identify → plan → deliver and hand over → sustain

questions.rationale: Benefits are identified, planned with owners and timing, delivered and handed over, then sustained.

option_rationales.a: This is precisely the failure pattern to avoid.
option_rationales.b: This describes project closure, not benefits realisation.
option_rationales.c: This is a commercial process, not a benefits process.
option_rationales.d: Benefits are identified, planned with owners and timing, delivered and handed over, then sustained.

questions.prompt: Which benefit goal is properly formulated?

options.text: 'Within 12 months, 40% of regional-ticket purchases run through the app and counter costs fall 15%'
'Improve the customer experience'
'Increase app usage significantly'
'Deliver the app by the agreed release date'

questions.rationale: A benefit goal needs a target value and a deadline, not a vague intention.

option_rationales.a: A benefit goal needs a target value and a deadline, not a vague intention.
option_rationales.b: No target value and no date.
option_rationales.c: 'Significantly' is not measurable.
option_rationales.d: A delivery date measures output, not benefit.

questions.prompt: When is value typically realised?

options.text: At the moment the deliverable is handed over
In use, after handover, once the outcome takes effect
At final acceptance sign-off
At the closing celebration

questions.rationale: Value materialises through adoption and use, usually after the project has closed.

option_rationales.a: Handover is the start of realisation, not realisation itself.
option_rationales.b: Value materialises through adoption and use, usually after the project has closed.
option_rationales.c: Acceptance confirms the output, not the value.
option_rationales.d: A celebration marks the end of the work, not the benefit.

questions.prompt: Low adoption of a delivered product is MOST likely a symptom of:

options.text: Poor technical quality alone
An excessive testing budget
Adoption and change measures that were never planned or measured
Too many stakeholders being consulted

questions.rationale: Without planned adoption measures and leading indicators, output rarely becomes benefit.

option_rationales.a: Technical quality alone rarely explains 8% adoption.
option_rationales.b: Testing effort does not suppress adoption.
option_rationales.c: Without planned adoption measures and leading indicators, output rarely becomes benefit.
option_rationales.d: Consulting stakeholders usually improves adoption.

questions.prompt: What exactly is an 'output' in the value chain?

options.text: The organisational change caused by the project
The stakeholder's satisfaction level
The financial return achieved
The deliverable the project produces

questions.rationale: The output is the deliverable itself; the change it causes is the outcome.

option_rationales.a: That describes the outcome.
option_rationales.b: That is a benefit measure, not the output.
option_rationales.c: That describes the value.
option_rationales.d: The output is the deliverable itself; the change it causes is the outcome.

questions.prompt: Governance, sustainability, business case and AI governance land FIRST in which ECO domain?

options.text: Business Environment
Process
People
They are examined separately

questions.rationale: These cross-cutting themes are anchored in the Business Environment domain.

option_rationales.a: These cross-cutting themes are anchored in the Business Environment domain.
option_rationales.b: Process covers the delivery mechanics.
option_rationales.c: People deals with teams, leadership and stakeholders.
option_rationales.d: They are blended into domain questions, not examined separately.

questions.prompt: How do cross-cutting themes typically appear in 2026 exam questions?

options.text: As clearly labelled standalone questions
Blended into scenarios, so one question can be both stakeholder and ethics/AI related
Only in the final section of the exam
Only in questions about agile delivery

questions.rationale: The exam deliberately mixes themes; a procurement question can also be a sustainability question.

option_rationales.a: They are not labelled as cross-cutting questions.
option_rationales.b: The exam deliberately mixes themes; a procurement question can also be a sustainability question.
option_rationales.c: They are distributed across the whole exam.
option_rationales.d: They apply to predictive work just as much.

questions.prompt: In PESTLE, an approval requirement from the national rail authority is which factor?

options.text: Legal
Economic
Political
Technological

questions.rationale: Statutory approvals, standards and procurement rules are Legal factors.

option_rationales.a: Statutory approvals, standards and procurement rules are Legal factors.
option_rationales.b: Economic covers prices, interest rates and budgets.
option_rationales.c: Political covers policy direction and funding programmes, not a specific approval.
option_rationales.d: Technological covers new technology and obsolescence.

questions.prompt: Mid-project, a new emissions rule tightens limits for site machinery, and two subcontractors' equipment no longer complies. This is primarily:

options.text: An organisational process asset the team failed to reuse
An enterprise environmental factor that a PESTLE scan should have flagged
A quality defect in the subcontractors' work
A scope change requested by the sponsor

questions.rationale: Regulations are conditions the team does not control — an EEF, and a Legal/Environmental PESTLE item.

option_rationales.a: OPAs are assets to reuse; a new regulation is not one.
option_rationales.b: Regulations are conditions the team does not control — an EEF, and a Legal/Environmental PESTLE item.
option_rationales.c: Nothing indicates defective work by the subcontractors.
option_rationales.d: The sponsor requested no change; the environment changed.

questions.prompt: Enterprise Environmental Factors (EEF) are best described as:

options.text: Templates and checklists the organisation reuses
Risks that have already occurred
Conditions the project does not control, which constrain it
Deliverables produced by the project

questions.rationale: EEFs are internal or external conditions (culture, market, regulation) that shape constraints and assumptions.

option_rationales.a: Templates and checklists are organisational process assets.
option_rationales.b: An occurred risk is an issue, not an EEF.
option_rationales.c: EEFs are internal or external conditions (culture, market, regulation) that shape constraints and assumptions.
option_rationales.d: Deliverables are project outputs, not environmental factors.

questions.prompt: Organisational Process Assets (OPA) are best described as:

options.text: Conditions the project must work within
The project's physical equipment
Assets purchased specifically for the project
Things the organisation owns and the project can reuse

questions.rationale: OPAs are processes, policies, templates, checklists, historical information and lessons learned.

option_rationales.a: Conditions to work within are enterprise environmental factors.
option_rationales.b: Physical equipment is a resource, not a process asset.
option_rationales.c: Purchased items are procurement, not process assets.
option_rationales.d: OPAs are processes, policies, templates, checklists, historical information and lessons learned.

questions.prompt: A lessons-learned database from previous station projects is:

options.text: An OPA
An EEF
A constraint
A stakeholder register

questions.rationale: Historical information and lessons learned are the classic organisational process asset.

option_rationales.a: Historical information and lessons learned are the classic organisational process asset.
option_rationales.b: EEFs are conditions you cannot change; a lessons database is yours to reuse.
option_rationales.c: A constraint limits options; this database enables them.
option_rationales.d: The stakeholder register is a project document, not an OPA.

questions.prompt: Steel market prices and interest rates are:

options.text: Internal EEFs
External EEFs
OPAs
Contingency reserves

questions.rationale: Market conditions and economic factors are external enterprise environmental factors.

option_rationales.a: Internal EEFs are conditions inside the organisation such as culture or systems.
option_rationales.b: Market conditions and economic factors are external enterprise environmental factors.
option_rationales.c: OPAs are reusable assets, not market conditions.
option_rationales.d: Reserves are budget provisions, not environmental factors.

questions.prompt: Company culture, organisational structure and existing IT systems are:

options.text: OPAs
External EEFs
Internal EEFs
Management reserves

questions.rationale: These are internal conditions the project must work within, so internal EEFs.

option_rationales.a: OPAs are reusable assets, not organisational conditions.
option_rationales.b: External EEFs sit outside the organisation, such as markets and regulation.
option_rationales.c: These are internal conditions the project must work within, so internal EEFs.
option_rationales.d: Reserves are budget provisions.

questions.prompt: Which simple test distinguishes an EEF from an OPA?

options.text: Is it expensive or cheap?
Is it documented or undocumented?
Is it internal or external?
Can I change it, or is it ours to reuse?

questions.rationale: If you cannot change it, it constrains you (EEF); if it is yours to reuse, it enables you (OPA).

option_rationales.a: Cost says nothing about whether something constrains or enables you.
option_rationales.b: Both EEFs and OPAs may be documented.
option_rationales.c: EEFs can be internal as well as external, so location does not decide it.
option_rationales.d: If you cannot change it, it constrains you (EEF); if it is yours to reuse, it enables you (OPA).

questions.prompt: Which PESTLE area is most often the blind spot that surprises projects mid-flight?

options.text: Political and Economic
Social and Technological
Legal and Environmental — pending rules that are not yet visible
None; PESTLE surprises are rare

questions.rationale: Pending legal and environmental changes typically land mid-project when nobody tracked them.

option_rationales.a: Political and economic shifts are usually visible and tracked.
option_rationales.b: Social and technological changes rarely land as sudden mid-project surprises.
option_rationales.c: Pending legal and environmental changes typically land mid-project when nobody tracked them.
option_rationales.d: Environmental surprises are common, which is why scanning exists.

questions.prompt: How often should the external environment be scanned?

options.text: Once, during initiation
Repeatedly, as a deliberate and recurring activity
Only when the sponsor requests it
Only at phase gates, by the steering committee

questions.rationale: A one-off scan goes stale; deliberate, repeated scanning is what prevents surprises.

option_rationales.a: A single scan at initiation goes stale within months.
option_rationales.b: A one-off scan goes stale; deliberate, repeated scanning is what prevents surprises.
option_rationales.c: Scanning is the project manager's job, not a sponsor request.
option_rationales.d: Gates are too infrequent to catch fast-moving external change.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of the project charter?

options.text: To define the detailed work breakdown structure
To record the final acceptance of deliverables
To authorise the project and empower the project manager
To list all identified risks

questions.rationale: The charter authorises the project, names the PM and links the work to the business case and strategy.

option_rationales.a: The WBS is produced later, during scope planning.
option_rationales.b: Acceptance is recorded at closing, not in the charter.
option_rationales.c: The charter authorises the project, names the PM and links the work to the business case and strategy.
option_rationales.d: Risks are recorded in the risk register.

questions.prompt: Which level decides that the organisation is doing the RIGHT projects?

options.text: The project
The programme
The project management office only
The portfolio

questions.rationale: Portfolio management selects and prioritises the right investments; programmes coordinate related projects.

option_rationales.a: The project delivers; it does not decide which projects are right.
option_rationales.b: Programmes coordinate related projects; selection sits above them.
option_rationales.c: A PMO may support portfolio decisions but does not replace them.
option_rationales.d: Portfolio management selects and prioritises the right investments; programmes coordinate related projects.

questions.prompt: A programme is best described as:

options.text: A group of related projects coordinated to obtain benefits not available individually
A very large project
A permanent operational department
A phase of the project life cycle

questions.rationale: Programmes coordinate related projects for collective benefit.

option_rationales.a: Programmes coordinate related projects for collective benefit.
option_rationales.b: Size alone does not make a project a programme.
option_rationales.c: Operational departments are permanent, not temporary endeavours.
option_rationales.d: A phase is part of one project's life cycle.

questions.prompt: Project governance primarily provides:

options.text: Detailed technical instructions to the team
A framework of decision rights, oversight and escalation
The project's budget
The list of deliverables

questions.rationale: Governance defines who decides what, with gates, reviews, escalation paths and accountability.

option_rationales.a: Technical instructions come from the team and its specifications.
option_rationales.b: Governance defines who decides what, with gates, reviews, escalation paths and accountability.
option_rationales.c: The budget is an input to governance, not governance itself.
option_rationales.d: Deliverables are defined by scope, not by governance.

questions.prompt: Compliance in a project context means:

options.text: Following the schedule baseline exactly
Doing whatever the sponsor requests
Adherence to laws, regulations and standards, evidenced and auditable
Meeting stakeholder expectations

questions.rationale: Compliance is about lawful, standard-conforming delivery with documented evidence.

option_rationales.a: Schedule adherence is performance, not compliance.
option_rationales.b: Sponsor requests are stakeholder expectations, not compliance.
option_rationales.c: Compliance is about lawful, standard-conforming delivery with documented evidence.
option_rationales.d: Expectations are managed; compliance is obeyed.

questions.prompt: A sponsor wants to skip the next gate — which includes a mandatory safety sign-off — to save three weeks. The project manager should:

options.text: Skip the gate, since the sponsor has the authority
Refuse to discuss it and simply proceed as planned
Skip the gate but document the decision in the risk register
Explain the risk and the rule, offer alternatives, and escalate through governance if needed

questions.rationale: Compliance is not traded for schedule; the accountable move is options plus escalation, not a flat no.

option_rationales.a: Sponsor authority does not override a mandatory safety sign-off.
option_rationales.b: Refusing without dialogue damages the relationship and solves nothing.
option_rationales.c: Documenting a knowing breach does not make it acceptable.
option_rationales.d: Compliance is not traded for schedule; the accountable move is options plus escalation, not a flat no.

questions.prompt: A phase gate is fundamentally:

options.text: A go/no-go decision point
A status update meeting
A contractual milestone for payment only
An internal team retrospective

questions.rationale: Gates make an explicit decision to continue, change or stop — not merely to report.

option_rationales.a: Gates make an explicit decision to continue, change or stop — not merely to report.
option_rationales.b: A status update reports; a gate decides.
option_rationales.c: Payment may be linked to a gate, but that is not its purpose.
option_rationales.d: A retrospective improves the team's process.

questions.prompt: A project is running without an approved charter. The main consequence is that:

options.text: The team cannot log risks
The project manager has no formal mandate or authority
No procurement can take place
The project cannot be added to the portfolio

questions.rationale: Without a charter, the PM's authority and the project's authorisation are undefined.

option_rationales.a: Risks can be logged with or without a charter.
option_rationales.b: Without a charter, the PM's authority and the project's authorisation are undefined.
option_rationales.c: Procurement is constrained by policy, not by the charter alone.
option_rationales.d: Portfolio inclusion happens before the charter is issued.

questions.prompt: A gate review and a hard deadline collide. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Silently postpone the gate
Ask the team to work overtime and say nothing
Escalate through the governance path with impact options
Cancel the deadline unilaterally

questions.rationale: Escalation via governance is a normal, healthy action — not an admission of failure.

option_rationales.a: Silently postponing hides a governance decision from those accountable.
option_rationales.b: Concealing the conflict is neither transparent nor sustainable.
option_rationales.c: Escalation via governance is a normal, healthy action — not an admission of failure.
option_rationales.d: The project manager cannot unilaterally cancel a sponsor's deadline.

questions.prompt: Which statement about compliance versus schedule pressure is correct?

options.text: Compliance may be deferred if the sponsor accepts the risk in writing
Compliance is a Process-domain topic, not Business Environment
Compliance applies only to externally funded projects
Compliance requirements are non-negotiable; a compliant path must be found

questions.rationale: The exam stance is unambiguous: you do not trade compliance away for speed.

option_rationales.a: Written acceptance of risk cannot authorise a breach of law or safety rules.
option_rationales.b: Compliance is explicitly part of the Business Environment domain.
option_rationales.c: Compliance applies to internally funded projects too.
option_rationales.d: The exam stance is unambiguous: you do not trade compliance away for speed.

questions.prompt: When choosing between projects, which value measure is generally the most complete?

options.text: Net Present Value
Payback period
Internal Rate of Return
Benefit-Cost Ratio

questions.rationale: NPV discounts all future cash flows to today and is the primary decision lens.

option_rationales.a: NPV discounts all future cash flows to today and is the primary decision lens.
option_rationales.b: Payback measures liquidity, ignoring value created after recovery.
option_rationales.c: IRR is useful but sensitive to cash-flow patterns and project scale.
option_rationales.d: BCR compares benefit to cost but does not express absolute value.

questions.prompt: Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is:

options.text: The ratio of benefits to costs
The discount rate at which NPV equals zero
The time needed to recover the investment
The net benefit divided by cost, as a percentage

questions.rationale: IRR is the rate where NPV = 0; higher is generally better.

option_rationales.a: That describes the benefit-cost ratio.
option_rationales.b: IRR is the rate where NPV = 0; higher is generally better.
option_rationales.c: That describes the payback period.
option_rationales.d: That describes return on investment.

questions.prompt: A Benefit-Cost Ratio of 0.8 means:

options.text: Benefits exceed costs by 80%
The project recovers its cost in 0.8 years
Benefits are less than costs — the project destroys value on this measure
The project has an 80% chance of success

questions.rationale: A BCR above 1 is good; 0.8 means costs outweigh benefits.

option_rationales.a: That would be a BCR of 1.8.
option_rationales.b: That describes a payback period, not a ratio.
option_rationales.c: A BCR above 1 is good; 0.8 means costs outweigh benefits.
option_rationales.d: BCR measures value, not probability of success.

questions.prompt: Which statement about payback period is correct?

options.text: Longer is better because it spreads risk
It accounts fully for the time value of money
It is the most complete measure of value
Shorter is better, but it ignores value created after payback

questions.rationale: Payback measures liquidity and speed of recovery; it is blind to later value.

option_rationales.a: A longer payback means capital is tied up longer.
option_rationales.b: Simple payback ignores the time value of money.
option_rationales.c: NPV is the more complete measure.
option_rationales.d: Payback measures liquidity and speed of recovery; it is blind to later value.

questions.prompt: Sunk cost should be treated how in a continue-or-stop decision?

options.text: Ignored — it is already spent and unrecoverable
Used to justify continuing so the money is not wasted
Added to remaining cost to show the full investment
Recovered from the supplier before deciding

questions.rationale: Only remaining cost versus remaining benefit is relevant to a forward decision.

option_rationales.a: Only remaining cost versus remaining benefit is relevant to a forward decision.
option_rationales.b: This is the sunk-cost fallacy the question is testing.
option_rationales.c: Adding sunk cost distorts a forward-looking decision.
option_rationales.d: Sunk cost is by definition unrecoverable.

questions.prompt: Project A: NPV EUR 1.2m, payback 4 years. Project B: NPV EUR 0.9m, payback 2 years. On value alone, which wins?

options.text: Project B
Project A
They are equivalent
Neither — NPV cannot be compared

questions.rationale: Higher NPV wins on value; payback becomes decisive only under liquidity constraints.

option_rationales.a: B has the lower NPV, so it loses on value.
option_rationales.b: Higher NPV wins on value; payback becomes decisive only under liquidity constraints.
option_rationales.c: Their NPVs differ by EUR 0.3m, so they are not equivalent.
option_rationales.d: NPVs are directly comparable — that is their purpose.

questions.prompt: In the same comparison, under what condition might Project B be preferred?

options.text: When the organisation wants the largest possible total value
When the discount rate is zero
When cash is tight and speed of recovery matters
When the projects have identical risk

questions.rationale: Payback is a liquidity check; tight cash can make faster recovery decisive.

option_rationales.a: Largest total value points to A, not B.
option_rationales.b: A zero discount rate would not favour faster recovery.
option_rationales.c: Payback is a liquidity check; tight cash can make faster recovery decisive.
option_rationales.d: Equal risk does not favour a shorter payback.

questions.prompt: A project has consumed EUR 4m of a EUR 5m budget, needs EUR 3m more, and the remaining benefits are now worth far less than EUR 3m. The rational recommendation is to:

options.text: Continue, because EUR 4m would otherwise be wasted
Continue, but reduce quality to save money
Transfer the project to another department
Stop or re-scope, based on remaining cost versus remaining benefit

questions.rationale: The EUR 4m is sunk; a negative forward business case justifies stopping or re-scoping.

option_rationales.a: This is the sunk-cost fallacy — the EUR 4m is irrecoverable.
option_rationales.b: Cutting quality to rescue a negative business case compounds the problem.
option_rationales.c: Moving a value-negative project elsewhere does not create value.
option_rationales.d: The EUR 4m is sunk; a negative forward business case justifies stopping or re-scoping.

questions.prompt: Which pair of metrics best covers both 'is it worth it?' and 'how soon do we recover?'

options.text: NPV and payback period
IRR and BCR
ROI and sunk cost
BCR and payback period

questions.rationale: NPV answers the value question; payback answers the liquidity question.

option_rationales.a: NPV answers the value question; payback answers the liquidity question.
option_rationales.b: Both IRR and BCR address worth, neither addresses liquidity.
option_rationales.c: Sunk cost is not a selection metric at all.
option_rationales.d: BCR and payback omit the absolute value measure.

questions.prompt: What is a 'value gate' in a business case?

options.text: A contractual penalty clause
A checkpoint where continuation depends on achieving agreed benefit measures
The final acceptance milestone
A budget ceiling set by finance

questions.rationale: Value gates fund value rather than momentum, and link the business case to governance.

option_rationales.a: Penalties are contractual, not business-case, mechanisms.
option_rationales.b: Value gates fund value rather than momentum, and link the business case to governance.
option_rationales.c: Final acceptance confirms output, not benefit.
option_rationales.d: A ceiling limits spend; it does not test value.

questions.prompt: A change request arrives. What should happen FIRST?

options.text: Implement it if it is small
Escalate it to the sponsor
Log it and assess its impact
Update the baselines

questions.rationale: Every request is logged and impact-assessed before any decision or implementation.

option_rationales.a: Implementing before assessment is exactly how control is lost.
option_rationales.b: Escalation comes after assessment, and only if needed.
option_rationales.c: Every request is logged and impact-assessed before any decision or implementation.
option_rationales.d: Baselines are updated only after approval.

questions.prompt: The Change Control Board (CCB) is responsible for:

options.text: Executing approved changes
Auditing the supplier's quality system
Writing the change requests
Approving, deferring or rejecting change requests

questions.rationale: The CCB decides; the team implements what is approved.

option_rationales.a: Implementation is done by the project team once approved.
option_rationales.b: Supplier quality audits are a procurement activity.
option_rationales.c: Requests are raised by whoever identifies the need.
option_rationales.d: The CCB decides; the team implements what is approved.

questions.prompt: After a change is approved, what MUST happen?

options.text: The baselines and affected plans are updated
The risk register is archived
The change is implemented without documentation to save time
The project is re-chartered

questions.rationale: Approved changes update the baselines; otherwise control of scope, cost and schedule is lost.

option_rationales.a: Approved changes update the baselines; otherwise control of scope, cost and schedule is lost.
option_rationales.b: The risk register stays live throughout the project.
option_rationales.c: Undocumented implementation destroys traceability.
option_rationales.d: Re-chartering is reserved for fundamental redefinition.

questions.prompt: Configuration management is primarily concerned with:

options.text: Changes to plans and baselines
Versions and status of the product and its components
The approval authority of the sponsor
The team's working agreements

questions.rationale: Configuration management ensures everyone works on the correct, current version of the thing.

option_rationales.a: Changes to plans and baselines are integrated change control.
option_rationales.b: Configuration management ensures everyone works on the correct, current version of the thing.
option_rationales.c: Approval authority is a governance matter.
option_rationales.d: Working agreements belong to the team charter.

questions.prompt: Integrated change control is primarily concerned with:

options.text: Versions of drawings and software builds
Supplier invoicing
Changes to plans and baselines, assessed and decided
Team performance appraisals

questions.rationale: Change control governs changes to baselines; configuration governs product versions.

option_rationales.a: Drawing and build versions are configuration management.
option_rationales.b: Invoicing is a procurement and finance activity.
option_rationales.c: Change control governs changes to baselines; configuration governs product versions.
option_rationales.d: Appraisals are a human-resources matter.

questions.prompt: A site engineer implements a small design tweak directly with the contractor. It works technically, but a later team installs equipment based on the old drawings and a clash occurs. What failed?

options.text: Only integrated change control
Only configuration management
Both — the change bypassed control and the as-built diverged from the approved version
Neither — this is a normal technical variation

questions.rationale: No request or impact assessment (change control) and an out-of-date baseline version (configuration).

option_rationales.a: Change control failed, but so did version management.
option_rationales.b: Configuration failed, but the change also bypassed assessment and approval.
option_rationales.c: No request or impact assessment (change control) and an out-of-date baseline version (configuration).
option_rationales.d: A change with no request and an outdated baseline is not a normal variation.

questions.prompt: Against which areas must every change request be assessed?

options.text: Scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk (and benefit/value)
Scope and cost only
Schedule and quality only
Whatever the requester considers relevant

questions.rationale: A complete impact assessment covers all constraint dimensions plus the value effect.

option_rationales.a: A complete impact assessment covers all constraint dimensions plus the value effect.
option_rationales.b: Scope and cost alone miss schedule, quality, risk and value effects.
option_rationales.c: Schedule and quality alone are incomplete.
option_rationales.d: Assessment scope cannot depend on the requester's preference.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order of the ADKAR model?

options.text: Ability, Desire, Knowledge, Awareness, Reinforcement
Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement
Awareness, Knowledge, Desire, Reinforcement, Ability
Desire, Awareness, Ability, Knowledge, Reinforcement

questions.rationale: ADKAR runs Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement.

option_rationales.a: Ability cannot come before awareness and knowledge.
option_rationales.b: ADKAR runs Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement.
option_rationales.c: Desire must precede knowledge, not follow it.
option_rationales.d: Awareness must come first, before desire.

questions.prompt: Which ADKAR element is about making the change stick over time?

options.text: Awareness
Knowledge
Reinforcement
Ability

questions.rationale: Reinforcement sustains the change; many change efforts fail precisely here.

option_rationales.a: Awareness explains why the change is needed.
option_rationales.b: Knowledge is about how to change.
option_rationales.c: Reinforcement sustains the change; many change efforts fail precisely here.
option_rationales.d: Ability is the skill to perform the new way.

questions.prompt: Why set approval thresholds for the project manager in a change process?

options.text: To avoid documenting small changes
To transfer accountability to the team
To remove the need for a CCB
To balance speed of delivery with retained control

questions.rationale: Thresholds let low-impact changes move quickly while larger ones go to the full CCB.

option_rationales.a: Every change is documented, whatever its size.
option_rationales.b: Accountability stays with the defined decision-makers.
option_rationales.c: Thresholds complement the CCB; they do not replace it.
option_rationales.d: Thresholds let low-impact changes move quickly while larger ones go to the full CCB.

questions.prompt: A risk is best defined as:

options.text: An uncertain event that, if it occurs, affects one or more objectives
A problem that has already occurred
Any negative event during the project
A gap between planned and actual cost

questions.rationale: Risk is uncertain and forward-looking; an occurred risk is an issue.

option_rationales.a: Risk is uncertain and forward-looking; an occurred risk is an issue.
option_rationales.b: An event that has occurred is an issue, not a risk.
option_rationales.c: Risk includes positive events as well as negative ones.
option_rationales.d: A cost variance is a measured result, not a risk.

questions.prompt: Which statement about risk is correct?

options.text: Risk is always negative
Risk can be negative (threat) or positive (opportunity)
Opportunities are not managed in projects
Only threats need response strategies

questions.rationale: Risk is neutral; opportunities are managed as deliberately as threats.

option_rationales.a: Risk is neutral and includes opportunities.
option_rationales.b: Risk is neutral; opportunities are managed as deliberately as threats.
option_rationales.c: Opportunities are managed with their own response strategies.
option_rationales.d: Opportunities require responses just as threats do.

questions.prompt: VUCA stands for:

options.text: Value, Uncertainty, Complexity, Adaptability
Volatility, Urgency, Capability, Ambiguity
Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity, Ambiguity
Variance, Uncertainty, Cost, Analysis

questions.rationale: VUCA names the conditions projects operate in: volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity.

option_rationales.a: Adaptability is not the 'A' in VUCA.
option_rationales.b: Urgency and capability are not part of the model.
option_rationales.c: VUCA names the conditions projects operate in: volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity.
option_rationales.d: Variance and cost belong to performance measurement.

questions.prompt: Which reserve is intended for unknown risks?

options.text: Contingency reserve
Profit margin
Cost baseline
Management reserve

questions.rationale: Contingency covers identified (known) risks; management reserve covers unknown risks.

option_rationales.a: Contingency reserve covers identified, analysed risks.
option_rationales.b: Profit margin is a commercial matter, not a project reserve.
option_rationales.c: The cost baseline excludes management reserve.
option_rationales.d: Contingency covers identified (known) risks; management reserve covers unknown risks.

questions.prompt: Contingency reserve is used for:

options.text: Identified risks that have been analysed
Unknown, unforeseeable events
Scope changes requested by the sponsor
Supplier profit adjustments

questions.rationale: Contingency is budgeted for known risks in the register.

option_rationales.a: Contingency is budgeted for known risks in the register.
option_rationales.b: Unknown risks are covered by management reserve.
option_rationales.c: Scope changes are funded through change control.
option_rationales.d: Supplier margin is a contractual matter.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a threat response strategy?

options.text: Avoid
Exploit
Transfer
Mitigate

questions.rationale: Exploit is an opportunity strategy; the threat set is avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept, escalate.

option_rationales.a: Avoid removes the cause of a threat.
option_rationales.b: Exploit is an opportunity strategy; the threat set is avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept, escalate.
option_rationales.c: Transfer shifts a threat to a third party.
option_rationales.d: Mitigate reduces a threat's probability or impact.

questions.prompt: Which opportunity strategy mirrors 'mitigate' for threats?

options.text: Exploit
Share
Enhance
Accept

questions.rationale: Mitigate reduces probability or impact of a threat; enhance increases them for an opportunity.

option_rationales.a: Exploit mirrors avoid — making certain the event occurs.
option_rationales.b: Share mirrors transfer — partnering to capture the upside.
option_rationales.c: Mitigate reduces probability or impact of a threat; enhance increases them for an opportunity.
option_rationales.d: Accept mirrors accept on both sides.

questions.prompt: A main steel supplier signals possible delivery delays due to raw-material shortages. Dual-sourcing and holding a buffer stock is which strategy?

options.text: Avoid
Escalate
Accept
Mitigate

questions.rationale: Reducing the probability or impact of the threat without removing the cause is mitigation.

option_rationales.a: Avoiding would mean removing the cause, e.g. changing the design entirely.
option_rationales.b: Escalation applies only if the response exceeds your authority.
option_rationales.c: Accepting would mean taking no action beyond holding reserve.
option_rationales.d: Reducing the probability or impact of the threat without removing the cause is mitigation.

questions.prompt: A neighbouring project offers to share a crane and specialist crew during your peak window. Coordinating actively to make this happen is:

options.text: Exploit
Accept
Enhance
Transfer

questions.rationale: Exploiting an opportunity means acting to ensure it actually occurs.

option_rationales.a: Exploiting an opportunity means acting to ensure it actually occurs.
option_rationales.b: Accepting would mean taking it only if it happened by itself.
option_rationales.c: Enhance increases probability or impact; here the opportunity is made certain.
option_rationales.d: Transfer is a threat strategy, not an opportunity strategy.

questions.prompt: When should a project manager escalate a risk?

options.text: Whenever the risk is negative
When the required response lies outside the project manager's authority
Only after the risk has occurred
Never — escalation signals weak project management

questions.rationale: Escalation is a governance action for risks beyond the PM's authority, not a failure.

option_rationales.a: Most negative risks are handled within the project.
option_rationales.b: Escalation is a governance action for risks beyond the PM's authority, not a failure.
option_rationales.c: Escalating after occurrence is too late to be a response.
option_rationales.d: Escalation is a legitimate governance action, not a weakness.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of Tuckman's team development stages?

options.text: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing
Forming, Norming, Storming, Performing
Storming, Forming, Norming, Performing
Forming, Storming, Performing, Norming

questions.rationale: Teams typically move Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing (then Adjourning).

option_rationales.a: Teams typically move Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing (then Adjourning).
option_rationales.b: Norming cannot precede storming; agreements form after friction surfaces.
option_rationales.c: Storming presupposes a formed group.
option_rationales.d: Norming precedes performing, not the reverse.

questions.prompt: A team is openly disagreeing about roles and technical approach. This most likely means:

options.text: The team is failing and members should be replaced
The team is in Storming — an uncomfortable but normal stage
The team has skipped Forming
The project manager has lost authority

questions.rationale: Storming is a healthy, expected stage; the PM coaches the team through it.

option_rationales.a: Replacing people treats a normal development stage as a personnel problem.
option_rationales.b: Storming is a healthy, expected stage; the PM coaches the team through it.
option_rationales.c: Storming follows forming; it does not replace it.
option_rationales.d: Open disagreement is not evidence of lost authority.

questions.prompt: Which leadership style best fits a newly formed team that is unsure of roles and purpose?

options.text: Delegating
Supporting
Directing
Laissez-faire

questions.rationale: A forming team needs clarity and direction; style shifts as the team matures.

option_rationales.a: Delegating assumes a mature, self-organising team.
option_rationales.b: Supporting suits a capable team that mainly needs facilitation.
option_rationales.c: A forming team needs clarity and direction; style shifts as the team matures.
option_rationales.d: Absent leadership leaves a new team without purpose or clarity.

questions.prompt: Which style best fits a mature, self-organising team in the Performing stage?

options.text: Directing
Coaching
Controlling
Delegating

questions.rationale: Performing teams need delegation and facilitation, not direction.

option_rationales.a: Directing a mature team wastes its capability and demotivates it.
option_rationales.b: Coaching suits a team still building skills and confidence.
option_rationales.c: Control is the opposite of what a performing team needs.
option_rationales.d: Performing teams need delegation and facilitation, not direction.

questions.prompt: A team charter is MOST effective when it is:

options.text: Co-created with the team so they own the agreements
Written by the project manager and distributed for information
Issued by the PMO as a standard template
Written by the sponsor to set expectations

questions.rationale: Ownership comes from writing it together; an imposed charter gets ignored.

option_rationales.a: Ownership comes from writing it together; an imposed charter gets ignored.
option_rationales.b: A charter handed over for information creates no ownership.
option_rationales.c: A standard template is a starting point, not the team's agreement.
option_rationales.d: Sponsor expectations belong in the project charter, not the team charter.

questions.prompt: Ground rules are best understood as:

options.text: Rules the project manager enforces on the team
Agreed behaviours the whole team upholds
Contractual obligations for external suppliers
Corporate policies that cannot be changed

questions.rationale: Ground rules are the team's own commitments, upheld collectively rather than policed by the PM.

option_rationales.a: PM enforcement turns agreements into imposed rules.
option_rationales.b: Ground rules are the team's own commitments, upheld collectively rather than policed by the PM.
option_rationales.c: Supplier duties are contractual, not team ground rules.
option_rationales.d: Corporate policies apply anyway; ground rules are the team's own.

questions.prompt: What is the primary challenge of virtual and distributed teams?

options.text: Higher tooling cost
Inability to use agile methods
Thinner communication and harder trust-building
Legal restrictions on remote work

questions.rationale: Communication, culture, time zones and trust are the recurring virtual-team challenges.

option_rationales.a: Tooling cost is minor beside communication and trust.
option_rationales.b: Agile works well in distributed settings with the right practices.
option_rationales.c: Communication, culture, time zones and trust are the recurring virtual-team challenges.
option_rationales.d: Remote work is legally normal in most contexts.

questions.prompt: In a hybrid team, on-site members dominate discussions while remote members go quiet. The BEST action is to:

options.text: Ask remote members to travel to the site more often
Accept it as a normal feature of distributed work
Reduce the number of joint meetings
Introduce inclusion practices such as round-robin input and documenting decisions in a shared space

questions.rationale: Structural inclusion measures neutralise the on-site/remote imbalance; good intentions alone do not.

option_rationales.a: Travel is expensive and does not fix the everyday imbalance.
option_rationales.b: Accepting exclusion wastes half the team's contribution.
option_rationales.c: Fewer joint meetings deepens the divide rather than closing it.
option_rationales.d: Structural inclusion measures neutralise the on-site/remote imbalance; good intentions alone do not.

questions.prompt: A skills gap exists but there is no budget for a formal course. Which option is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Pairing, mentoring or job shadowing with experienced colleagues
Postpone the work until training funds appear
Hire a replacement specialist
Ignore the gap and monitor quality closely

questions.rationale: Competency development need not be expensive; pairing and mentoring are legitimate routes.

option_rationales.a: Competency development need not be expensive; pairing and mentoring are legitimate routes.
option_rationales.b: Postponing work does not develop anyone.
option_rationales.c: Replacing people is costly and ignores existing potential.
option_rationales.d: Ignoring a known gap makes defects likely.

questions.prompt: A newly inherited team is polite in meetings but nothing moves, decisions are re-litigated and there is no charter. What should the project manager do FIRST?

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor about a difficult team
Co-create a team charter and ground rules with the team
Reassign the two members who disagree
Increase the frequency of status reporting

questions.rationale: The absence of agreements is the root cause; co-created agreements address it directly.

option_rationales.a: Escalating before using your own tools looks like avoidance.
option_rationales.b: The absence of agreements is the root cause; co-created agreements address it directly.
option_rationales.c: Separating people avoids the disagreement rather than resolving it.
option_rationales.d: More reporting measures the problem instead of solving it.

questions.prompt: Servant leadership means the project manager primarily:

options.text: Commands and controls the team's work
Delegates all accountability to the team
Serves the team by removing impediments and growing people
Avoids making any decisions

questions.rationale: Servant leaders clear obstacles, coach and enable a self-organising team.

option_rationales.a: Command and control is the opposite of servant leadership.
option_rationales.b: Accountability stays with the project manager.
option_rationales.c: Servant leaders clear obstacles, coach and enable a self-organising team.
option_rationales.d: Servant leaders still decide; they simply decide differently.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour most undermines a project manager's credibility?

options.text: Asking the team for input on decisions
Admitting they do not know a technical answer
Escalating a risk beyond their authority
Demanding quality but cutting corners themselves under pressure

questions.rationale: Leading by example is central; behaviour, not rhetoric, is the real message.

option_rationales.a: Asking for input strengthens credibility.
option_rationales.b: Admitting a knowledge gap builds trust rather than eroding it.
option_rationales.c: Escalating an out-of-scope risk is appropriate governance.
