option_rationales.d: Leading by example is central; behaviour, not rhetoric, is the real message.

questions.prompt: A specialist who does not report to you keeps deprioritising your project for line work. What should you do FIRST?

options.text: Speak directly with the specialist to understand the priority conflict
Escalate to the sponsor
Ask their line manager to instruct them
Replace them with another resource

questions.rationale: Understand before escalating; the direct conversation is both faster and more respectful.

option_rationales.a: Understand before escalating; the direct conversation is both faster and more respectful.
option_rationales.b: Escalation before understanding skips the cheapest, most respectful step.
option_rationales.c: Instructing through a manager produces compliance, not commitment.
option_rationales.d: Replacing a scarce specialist is rarely realistic and signals poor leadership.

questions.prompt: A capable, mature squad keeps asking you to sign off trivial decisions. The BEST response is to:

options.text: Continue signing off to maintain control
Delegate the decisions back to them with clear boundaries
Introduce a formal approval workflow
Escalate the behaviour to their line managers

questions.rationale: Over-reliance signals under-delegation; empowering them frees you and grows them.

option_rationales.a: Continuing to sign off entrenches the dependency.
option_rationales.b: Over-reliance signals under-delegation; empowering them frees you and grows them.
option_rationales.c: A formal workflow adds bureaucracy to a delegation problem.
option_rationales.d: The behaviour is a leadership issue, not a performance complaint.

questions.prompt: A brand-new hire is overwhelmed and making errors. The BEST leadership response is to:

options.text: Delegate more so they learn quickly
Move them off the project
Direct and coach: clear priorities, pairing and a short feedback loop
Increase their workload to build resilience

questions.rationale: A forming individual needs direction and coaching; delegation here sets them up to fail.

option_rationales.a: Delegation without support sets a new hire up to fail.
option_rationales.b: Removal wastes the investment and ignores the real need.
option_rationales.c: A forming individual needs direction and coaching; delegation here sets them up to fail.
option_rationales.d: More work compounds the overload.

questions.prompt: Without formal authority, a project manager's influence comes mainly from:

options.text: The org chart
The sponsor's willingness to issue instructions
Control of the budget alone
Relationships, shared purpose, credibility and reciprocity

questions.rationale: Influence in a matrix comes from trust and purpose rather than reporting lines.

option_rationales.a: The org chart is precisely what is missing in this situation.
option_rationales.b: Borrowed authority is fragile and creates resentment.
option_rationales.c: Budget alone rarely moves people who do not report to you.
option_rationales.d: Influence in a matrix comes from trust and purpose rather than reporting lines.

questions.prompt: In People-domain scenarios, escalation should generally be:

options.text: A backstop after direct conversation and collaboration have been tried
The first action, to protect the schedule
Avoided entirely under all circumstances
Used whenever a team member disagrees with you

questions.rationale: Leading with escalation is the classic wrong answer; understand and collaborate first.

option_rationales.a: Leading with escalation is the classic wrong answer; understand and collaborate first.
option_rationales.b: Escalating first signals you cannot manage your own team.
option_rationales.c: Some issues genuinely exceed the project manager's authority.
option_rationales.d: Disagreement is healthy and is not an escalation trigger.

questions.prompt: Situational leadership implies that leadership style should follow:

options.text: The project manager's personal preference
The maturity of the team and the demands of the situation
The organisation's standard policy
The size of the project budget

questions.rationale: Style is a dial that tracks team maturity and context, not a fixed trait.

option_rationales.a: Personal preference produces one fixed style, applied regardless of need.
option_rationales.b: Style is a dial that tracks team maturity and context, not a fixed trait.
option_rationales.c: A standard policy cannot anticipate every team situation.
option_rationales.d: Budget size says nothing about how a team should be led.

questions.prompt: 'Be an Accountable Leader' in a matrix organisation means:

options.text: Accountability applies only where you have line authority
Accountability transfers to the functional managers
You remain accountable for outcomes regardless of formal authority
Accountability rests solely with the sponsor

questions.rationale: PMs are accountable across functions and contractors without commanding them.

option_rationales.a: Accountability in a matrix does not depend on line authority.
option_rationales.b: Functional managers own people, not project outcomes.
option_rationales.c: PMs are accountable across functions and contractors without commanding them.
option_rationales.d: The sponsor is accountable for benefits, not for daily delivery.

questions.prompt: Which of these is LEAST consistent with servant leadership?

options.text: Shielding the team from shifting priorities
Coaching a struggling team member
Removing an approval blocker for the team
Issuing detailed instructions on how each task must be done

questions.rationale: Micromanaging how work is done contradicts facilitating and empowering.

option_rationales.a: Shielding the team from churn is a core servant-leader duty.
option_rationales.b: Coaching is central to growing the team.
option_rationales.c: Removing blockers is the clearest expression of servant leadership.
option_rationales.d: Micromanaging how work is done contradicts facilitating and empowering.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of Goleman's five components of emotional intelligence?

options.text: Delegation
Self-management
Self-awareness
Empathy

questions.rationale: The five are self-awareness, self-management, motivation, empathy and social skill.

option_rationales.a: The five are self-awareness, self-management, motivation, empathy and social skill.
option_rationales.b: Self-management builds directly on self-awareness.
option_rationales.c: Self-awareness is the foundational component.
option_rationales.d: Empathy is the fourth component.

questions.prompt: Why are self-awareness and self-management considered foundational?

options.text: They are easier to learn than the others
You cannot read a room accurately while your own reaction is running you
They are the only components measured in appraisals
They apply only to senior leaders

questions.rationale: Managing your own reaction is a precondition for empathy and effective social skill.

option_rationales.a: Difficulty of learning is not the reason for the sequence.
option_rationales.b: Managing your own reaction is a precondition for empathy and effective social skill.
option_rationales.c: Appraisal practice has nothing to do with the model.
option_rationales.d: Emotional intelligence applies at every level.

questions.prompt: Empathy in a project context means:

options.text: Agreeing with stakeholders to keep the peace
Avoiding difficult conversations
Accurately reading others' emotions and perspectives
Sharing personal information to build rapport

questions.rationale: Empathy is accurate perception of others' emotions — not agreement or avoidance.

option_rationales.a: Agreement to keep the peace is smoothing, not empathy.
option_rationales.b: Avoidance is the opposite of engaging with emotion.
option_rationales.c: Empathy is accurate perception of others' emotions — not agreement or avoidance.
option_rationales.d: Self-disclosure is not the same as reading others.

questions.prompt: A contractor blames your organisation in a heated review. Pausing to notice your own defensiveness before responding is an example of:

options.text: Empathy
Motivation
Social skill
Self-management

questions.rationale: Choosing your response rather than reacting automatically is self-regulation.

option_rationales.a: Empathy would be reading the contractor's emotion, not your own.
option_rationales.b: Motivation concerns inner drive toward goals.
option_rationales.c: Social skill is what you do after regulating yourself.
option_rationales.d: Choosing your response rather than reacting automatically is self-regulation.

questions.prompt: According to Herzberg, salary and working conditions are:

options.text: Hygiene factors that prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate
Motivators that drive engagement
Irrelevant to employee behaviour
The strongest predictors of performance

questions.rationale: Hygiene factors remove dissatisfaction; motivation comes from achievement, recognition and growth.

option_rationales.a: Hygiene factors remove dissatisfaction; motivation comes from achievement, recognition and growth.
option_rationales.b: Motivators are achievement, recognition, meaningful work and growth.
option_rationales.c: Hygiene factors matter — get them wrong and people are dissatisfied.
option_rationales.d: Pay predicts dissatisfaction far better than it predicts performance.

questions.prompt: Which set best describes intrinsic motivators for knowledge work?

options.text: Bonus, company car, job title
Autonomy, mastery, purpose
Overtime pay, flexible hours, parking
Job security, pension, insurance

questions.rationale: Autonomy, mastery and purpose outperform extrinsic rewards for knowledge work.

option_rationales.a: These are extrinsic rewards and hygiene factors.
option_rationales.b: Autonomy, mastery and purpose outperform extrinsic rewards for knowledge work.
option_rationales.c: These are working conditions, i.e. hygiene factors.
option_rationales.d: These are security-related hygiene factors.

questions.prompt: A strong performer has become withdrawn after being passed over for a role. What should the project manager do FIRST?

options.text: Offer a bonus to restore motivation
Open a performance-management conversation
Hold a one-to-one with open questions and genuinely listen
Reassign them to less demanding work

questions.rationale: Understand before acting; the flatness is a signal, not a discipline issue.

option_rationales.a: Money misses the point when the need is recognition and growth.
option_rationales.b: Treating a motivation dip as underperformance damages trust.
option_rationales.c: Understand before acting; the flatness is a signal, not a discipline issue.
option_rationales.d: Reducing the challenge removes mastery, deepening the disengagement.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes empowerment from simple delegation?

options.text: Empowerment transfers real decision authority, not just tasks
Empowerment applies only to agile teams
Empowerment removes the project manager's accountability
There is no practical difference

questions.rationale: Handing over tasks while retaining all decisions is not empowerment.

option_rationales.a: Handing over tasks while retaining all decisions is not empowerment.
option_rationales.b: Empowerment applies in predictive settings too.
option_rationales.c: The project manager remains accountable for outcomes.
option_rationales.d: The difference is decisive: authority versus tasks.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between mentoring and coaching?

options.text: A mentor shares experience and opens doors; a coach asks questions to unlock the person's own answers
Mentoring is formal; coaching is informal
Coaching is only for underperformers
Mentoring applies only to new hires

questions.rationale: Mentors advise from experience; coaches ask rather than tell.

option_rationales.a: Mentors advise from experience; coaches ask rather than tell.
option_rationales.b: Both can be formal or informal.
option_rationales.c: Coaching is for everyone, not a remedial measure.
option_rationales.d: Mentoring benefits experienced people as well.

questions.prompt: Which action is MOST likely to re-engage a demotivated specialist whose need is recognition and growth?

options.text: A one-off cash bonus
Ownership of a meaningful workstream with real decision authority
More frequent status check-ins
A public apology from the sponsor

questions.rationale: Money rarely fixes a recognition problem; autonomy, mastery and purpose do.

option_rationales.a: A one-off payment does not address a recognition need.
option_rationales.b: Money rarely fixes a recognition problem; autonomy, mastery and purpose do.
option_rationales.c: More check-ins can feel like surveillance, not recognition.
option_rationales.d: An apology does not restore purpose or growth.

questions.prompt: Which conflict-handling mode generally produces the best and most durable outcome?

options.text: Compromise
Smooth / Accommodate
Collaborate / Confront
Force / Compete

questions.rationale: Collaborating problem-solves toward a win-win and is the exam's preferred default.

option_rationales.a: Compromise is fast but leaves both sides partly dissatisfied.
option_rationales.b: Smoothing preserves harmony at the cost of the better solution.
option_rationales.c: Collaborating problem-solves toward a win-win and is the exam's preferred default.
option_rationales.d: Forcing is quick but breeds resentment.

questions.prompt: Which mode is characterised by both parties giving something up, leaving neither fully satisfied?

options.text: Collaborate
Force
Avoid
Compromise

questions.rationale: Compromise is quick and fair-seeming but only partially satisfies both sides.

option_rationales.a: Collaborating seeks a solution that satisfies both fully.
option_rationales.b: Forcing means one side gives up everything.
option_rationales.c: Avoiding means no one gives anything — the issue is deferred.
option_rationales.d: Compromise is quick and fair-seeming but only partially satisfies both sides.

questions.prompt: Emphasising areas of agreement and yielding on your own point to preserve harmony is:

options.text: Smoothing / Accommodating
Avoiding
Forcing
Collaborating

questions.rationale: Smoothing yields the point, which is reasonable when the issue matters far more to the other party.

option_rationales.a: Smoothing yields the point, which is reasonable when the issue matters far more to the other party.
option_rationales.b: Avoiding steps away from the issue entirely.
option_rationales.c: Forcing pushes your own position through.
option_rationales.d: Collaborating works the problem rather than yielding.

questions.prompt: Pushing your position through against opposition is:

options.text: Compromising
Forcing / Competing
Collaborating
Accommodating

questions.rationale: Forcing is fast but breeds resentment; use it sparingly, e.g. for safety or ethics.

option_rationales.a: Compromising involves mutual concessions.
option_rationales.b: Forcing is fast but breeds resentment; use it sparingly, e.g. for safety or ethics.
option_rationales.c: Collaborating seeks a joint solution.
option_rationales.d: Accommodating means yielding your own position.

questions.prompt: Postponing a disagreement or stepping back from it entirely is:

options.text: Compromising
Smoothing
Avoiding / Withdrawing
Collaborating

questions.rationale: Avoiding can buy time to gather facts, but usually just defers the problem.

option_rationales.a: Compromising means both sides concede something now.
option_rationales.b: Smoothing emphasises agreement rather than withdrawing.
option_rationales.c: Avoiding can buy time to gather facts, but usually just defers the problem.
option_rationales.d: Collaborating engages directly with the problem.

questions.prompt: Two respected technical leads are dug in over an architecture decision that is now overdue. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Decide the architecture personally to save time
Postpone the decision until tempers cool
Split the difference between both designs
Facilitate agreement on objective criteria first, then evaluate options against them

questions.rationale: Agreeing criteria before options depersonalises the decision and is the essence of collaborating.

option_rationales.a: Deciding personally may pick the weaker design and alienate a respected lead.
option_rationales.b: The decision is already overdue; delay is now the problem.
option_rationales.c: Splitting the difference can produce an architecture that satisfies neither need.
option_rationales.d: Agreeing criteria before options depersonalises the decision and is the essence of collaborating.

questions.prompt: When should conflict be addressed?

options.text: Early and directly, at the lowest level possible
Only after it has affected the schedule
Only in formal retrospectives
Only when a stakeholder complains

questions.rationale: Early, direct handling at the lowest level is the consistent exam preference.

option_rationales.a: Early, direct handling at the lowest level is the consistent exam preference.
option_rationales.b: Waiting for schedule impact means acting far too late.
option_rationales.c: Retrospectives are too infrequent for live conflict.
option_rationales.d: Waiting for a complaint lets the conflict harden.

questions.prompt: In principled negotiation, the negotiator should focus on:

options.text: Positions, to hold a firm line
Interests, to find options for mutual gain
Personalities, to build rapport
Precedents, to justify the outcome

questions.rationale: A position is what someone says they want; the interest is why — and it unlocks options.

option_rationales.a: Positions are what people say they want; interests explain why.
option_rationales.b: A position is what someone says they want; the interest is why — and it unlocks options.
option_rationales.c: Personal rapport helps but does not resolve substantive conflict.
option_rationales.d: Precedents can inform criteria but are not the focus.

questions.prompt: What is a BATNA?

options.text: The budget authority for negotiated agreements
A binding arbitration clause
Your best alternative if no agreement is reached
The other party's opening offer

questions.rationale: Knowing your BATNA tells you when to walk away and prevents accepting a poor deal.

option_rationales.a: BATNA is not an approval limit.
option_rationales.b: Arbitration is a dispute mechanism, not an alternative you hold.
option_rationales.c: Knowing your BATNA tells you when to walk away and prevents accepting a poor deal.
option_rationales.d: Their opening offer is a position, not your alternative.

questions.prompt: Why use objective criteria in a negotiation?

options.text: To speed the negotiation by removing discussion
To satisfy audit requirements
To transfer the decision to a third party
To make the outcome fair and defensible rather than a contest of wills

questions.rationale: Benchmarks, standards and data keep the agreement fair, durable and depersonalised.

option_rationales.a: Criteria structure the discussion rather than removing it.
option_rationales.b: Audit needs are a by-product, not the purpose.
option_rationales.c: The decision stays with the parties.
option_rationales.d: Benchmarks, standards and data keep the agreement fair, durable and depersonalised.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly describes stakeholder engagement levels?

options.text: Unaware, Resistant, Neutral, Supportive, Leading
Resistant, Unaware, Neutral, Leading, Supportive
Unaware, Neutral, Resistant, Supportive, Leading
Neutral, Unaware, Supportive, Resistant, Leading

questions.rationale: The spectrum runs unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading.

option_rationales.a: The spectrum runs unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading.
option_rationales.b: Unaware must precede resistant — you cannot resist what you do not know.
option_rationales.c: Resistant sits between unaware and neutral.
option_rationales.d: Unaware is the starting point of the spectrum.

questions.prompt: How should the engagement-level spectrum be used?

options.text: To rank stakeholders by seniority
To assess current versus desired engagement and plan actions to close the gap
To decide who receives the status report
To calculate stakeholder-related risk reserves

questions.rationale: Engagement planning is a deliberate gap-closing activity per key stakeholder.

option_rationales.a: Seniority is not the same as engagement level.
option_rationales.b: Engagement planning is a deliberate gap-closing activity per key stakeholder.
option_rationales.c: Distribution lists are an output, not the purpose.
option_rationales.d: Reserves are a cost and risk mechanism.

questions.prompt: The purpose of a power/interest grid is to:

options.text: Record stakeholder contact details
Assign work packages to stakeholders
Prioritise where to spend limited engagement effort
Measure stakeholder satisfaction

questions.rationale: Analysis tools direct engagement energy toward the stakeholders who matter most.

option_rationales.a: Contact details belong in the stakeholder register.
option_rationales.b: Stakeholders receive engagement, not work packages.
option_rationales.c: Analysis tools direct engagement energy toward the stakeholders who matter most.
option_rationales.d: Satisfaction is measured separately, after engagement.

questions.prompt: The team has been blocked for a week awaiting an external sign-off. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the team to work around the blocker
Log it as a risk and continue reporting
Reassign the team to other projects
Take active ownership of removing the blocker, escalating if it exceeds their authority

questions.rationale: Actively clearing the path is the most concrete expression of servant leadership.

option_rationales.a: Working around a blocker wastes capacity and hides the issue.
option_rationales.b: Logging without acting leaves the team blocked.
option_rationales.c: Reassigning the team abandons the work rather than unblocking it.
option_rationales.d: Actively clearing the path is the most concrete expression of servant leadership.

questions.prompt: Sprint metrics show 'green' because blocked work is simply not counted. This is primarily:

options.text: A measurement failure that hides the problem from those who could help
An acceptable simplification for executive reporting
A configuration management error
A procurement compliance issue

questions.rationale: Honest metrics must make blocked work and cycle time visible; a flattering metric conceals risk.

option_rationales.a: Honest metrics must make blocked work and cycle time visible; a flattering metric conceals risk.
option_rationales.b: Comfortable metrics that conceal blocked work mislead decision-makers.
option_rationales.c: No product versioning issue is described.
option_rationales.d: No supplier or contract issue is involved.

questions.prompt: What makes escalation a professional rather than a reactive act?

options.text: Escalating as soon as any problem appears
Escalating according to a pre-agreed trigger after a direct attempt has failed
Escalating only when the sponsor asks
Never escalating without written approval from the team

questions.rationale: A rule-based trigger prevents both premature escalation and endless waiting.

option_rationales.a: Escalating every problem overloads governance and erodes credibility.
option_rationales.b: A rule-based trigger prevents both premature escalation and endless waiting.
option_rationales.c: Waiting to be asked leaves the team blocked indefinitely.
option_rationales.d: Team approval is not a prerequisite for escalation.

questions.prompt: Which recognition practice is both effective and essentially free?

options.text: An annual bonus scheme
Additional annual leave
Timely, specific, public recognition of good work
A promotion to a higher grade

questions.rationale: Recognition and specific feedback are powerful motivators at no cost.

option_rationales.a: A bonus scheme is costly and slow, and is a hygiene factor.
option_rationales.b: Extra leave has a real cost and is not immediate.
option_rationales.c: Recognition and specific feedback are powerful motivators at no cost.
option_rationales.d: Promotion is rarely within the project manager's gift.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of a retrospective is to:

options.text: Report status to the sponsor
Assess individual performance for appraisals
Demonstrate the product to stakeholders
Improve how the team works, continuously

questions.rationale: Retrospectives are the team's own continuous-improvement mechanism.

option_rationales.a: Status reporting is a different event with a different audience.
option_rationales.b: Individual appraisal would destroy the psychological safety a retrospective needs.
option_rationales.c: Demonstrating the product is the review's purpose.
option_rationales.d: Retrospectives are the team's own continuous-improvement mechanism.

questions.prompt: Building 'shared understanding' with stakeholders mainly aims to:

options.text: Surface and resolve misalignment on goals early
Reduce the number of meetings
Transfer responsibility for scope decisions
Satisfy documentation requirements

questions.rationale: Shared understanding prevents misalignment exploding later at a gate review.

option_rationales.a: Shared understanding prevents misalignment exploding later at a gate review.
option_rationales.b: Fewer meetings may follow, but that is not the aim.
option_rationales.c: Responsibility for scope stays where governance assigns it.
option_rationales.d: Documentation is a means, not the objective.

questions.prompt: A key stakeholder never attends meetings and does not reply to messages. What should the project manager do FIRST?

options.text: Escalate to their superior immediately
Attempt direct, low-friction engagement to understand their constraints and make the ask concrete
Continue sending the same meeting invitations
Proceed without their input and document the fact

questions.rationale: Proactive direct engagement precedes escalation; another ignored invite changes nothing.

option_rationales.a: Escalating first skips the cheapest and most respectful step.
option_rationales.b: Proactive direct engagement precedes escalation; another ignored invite changes nothing.
option_rationales.c: Repeating an ignored invitation changes nothing.
option_rationales.d: Proceeding without a key stakeholder invites later rework.

questions.prompt: A station rebuild has a fixed design, strict safety approvals and stable requirements. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Predictive
Agile
Pure Scrum
Kanban only

questions.rationale: Stable scope and heavy compliance favour a predictive approach with upfront planning and controlled change.

option_rationales.a: Stable scope and heavy compliance favour a predictive approach with upfront planning and controlled change.
option_rationales.b: Agile suits evolving requirements, not a fixed design under safety approval.
option_rationales.c: Scrum is an agile framework and fits discovery work, not fixed civil design.
option_rationales.d: Kanban alone provides no upfront plan for approvals and phasing.

questions.prompt: A passenger app's features are still being discovered with users. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Predictive
Agile
Waterfall with change control
Fixed-scope contract delivery

questions.rationale: Evolving requirements and a need for feedback favour iterative, incremental delivery.

option_rationales.a: Predictive planning would freeze features that are still being discovered.
option_rationales.b: Evolving requirements and a need for feedback favour iterative, incremental delivery.
option_rationales.c: Waterfall with change control makes every discovery a costly change.
option_rationales.d: Fixed scope contradicts requirements that are still emerging.

questions.prompt: One programme contains safety-critical civil works and a discovery-driven software product. The BEST structure is:

options.text: Force agile onto both for consistency
Force predictive onto both for reporting simplicity
A hybrid: predictive for the civil works, agile for the software, with defined integration points
Split them into two unrelated programmes

questions.rationale: Hybrid lets each workstream use the fitting method while integration points keep them aligned.

option_rationales.a: Forcing agile onto safety-critical civil works undermines approvals and planning.
option_rationales.b: Forcing predictive onto discovery work suppresses the feedback the product needs.
option_rationales.c: Hybrid lets each workstream use the fitting method while integration points keep them aligned.
option_rationales.d: Splitting them loses the integration points that make the programme coherent.

questions.prompt: PMBOK 8 is described as 'non-prescriptive'. For the project manager this means:

options.text: Processes are optional and may be ignored
Documentation is no longer required
Only agile methods are now supported
The PM selects and tailors processes to fit the project context

questions.rationale: Non-prescriptive means fitting the process to the work, with justification.

option_rationales.a: Non-prescriptive means selecting deliberately, not ignoring process.
option_rationales.b: Documentation is right-sized, not abolished.
option_rationales.c: Both predictive and agile approaches remain fully supported.
option_rationales.d: Non-prescriptive means fitting the process to the work, with justification.

questions.prompt: Tailoring should be driven by:

options.text: The value each process adds relative to the project's risk and context
The project manager's personal preference
The desire to minimise documentation in all cases
Whatever the last project did

questions.rationale: Keep what adds value, drop pure ceremony — always with a reason tied to context.

option_rationales.a: Keep what adds value, drop pure ceremony — always with a reason tied to context.
option_rationales.b: Preference is not a justification the exam accepts.
option_rationales.c: Sometimes more documentation is exactly what the risk requires.
option_rationales.d: Copying the last project ignores this project's context.

questions.prompt: Which element must NOT be tailored away, whatever the method?

options.text: Daily stand-ups
Governance and compliance requirements
Detailed upfront documentation
Formal status reports

questions.rationale: Tailoring reduces waste but never removes oversight or statutory obligations.

option_rationales.a: Stand-ups are valuable but can be tailored in predictive settings.
option_rationales.b: Tailoring reduces waste but never removes oversight or statutory obligations.
option_rationales.c: Heavy upfront documentation is a prime candidate for tailoring.
option_rationales.d: Reporting format is tailorable; the obligation to report is not.

questions.prompt: A sponsor demands 'one consistent method for the whole programme' purely for reporting simplicity. The BEST response is:

options.text: Comply, since the sponsor sets the method
Refuse and continue without explanation
Explain that reporting can be unified while delivery mechanics differ by workstream
Escalate to the portfolio board immediately

questions.rationale: Separate what must be uniform (reporting, governance) from what should vary (delivery mechanics).

option_rationales.a: Complying harms whichever workstream gets the wrong method.
option_rationales.b: Refusing without explanation damages the relationship and resolves nothing.
option_rationales.c: Separate what must be uniform (reporting, governance) from what should vary (delivery mechanics).
option_rationales.d: Escalation is premature before the trade-off has been explained.

questions.prompt: Tailoring is best understood as:

options.text: A one-off decision made during initiation
Something done only when a project is in trouble
A task owned solely by the PMO
An ongoing activity as the project learns

questions.rationale: Tailoring continues throughout, adapting as context and knowledge change.

option_rationales.a: A one-off decision cannot reflect what the project later learns.
option_rationales.b: Tailoring is a normal practice, not a rescue measure.
option_rationales.c: The PMO may advise, but the project manager tailors.
option_rationales.d: Tailoring continues throughout, adapting as context and knowledge change.

questions.prompt: In a predictive project, deliverables are decomposed into manageable work packages using:

options.text: The work breakdown structure
The product backlog
The risk register
The stakeholder register

questions.rationale: The WBS decomposes deliverables into work packages, and the scope baseline is then set.

option_rationales.a: The WBS decomposes deliverables into work packages, and the scope baseline is then set.
option_rationales.b: The backlog is the agile equivalent, not the predictive one.
option_rationales.c: The risk register records risks, not scope decomposition.
option_rationales.d: The stakeholder register records people, not deliverables.

questions.prompt: In an agile project, scope is primarily expressed as:

options.text: A frozen scope statement
A prioritised product backlog, continuously refined
A signed requirements specification
A work breakdown structure baselined at kickoff

questions.rationale: Agile uses a living, prioritised backlog with acceptance criteria per item.

option_rationales.a: A frozen statement contradicts continuous refinement.
option_rationales.b: Agile uses a living, prioritised backlog with acceptance criteria per item.
option_rationales.c: Signed specifications belong to predictive contracting.
option_rationales.d: A baselined WBS is the predictive structure.

questions.prompt: The purpose of an MVP is to:

options.text: Deliver the cheapest possible product
Reduce the team size
Deliver the smallest release that provides real value and validates assumptions early
Avoid the need for acceptance criteria

questions.rationale: An MVP creates early value and learning rather than minimising quality.

option_rationales.a: Cheapness is not the aim; validated value is.
option_rationales.b: Team size is unrelated to the MVP concept.
option_rationales.c: An MVP creates early value and learning rather than minimising quality.
option_rationales.d: Acceptance criteria are needed for MVP items too.

questions.prompt: Progressive elaboration means:

options.text: Adding scope gradually without approval
Increasing documentation with each phase
Delaying all planning until requirements are complete
Planning in detail only as far as you can reliably see, elaborating as you learn

questions.rationale: Detail emerges over time; you plan to the horizon you can see.

option_rationales.a: Adding scope without approval is scope creep, not elaboration.
option_rationales.b: The volume of documentation is not what elaborates.
option_rationales.c: Waiting for complete requirements would stall the project indefinitely.
option_rationales.d: Detail emerges over time; you plan to the horizon you can see.

questions.prompt: Stakeholders keep adding 'tiny' features directly to developers in the corridor, consuming three sprints. The core problem is:

options.text: The changes bypassed the process, so there is no visibility, assessment or trade-off
The features were too large
The team worked too slowly
The backlog was too short

questions.rationale: Creep is a process failure about the route a change takes, not about its size.

option_rationales.a: Creep is a process failure about the route a change takes, not about its size.
option_rationales.b: Each change was small; the accumulation and the route were the problem.
option_rationales.c: The team delivered well; capacity was consumed by unmanaged additions.
option_rationales.d: Backlog length is not the issue.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes valid change from scope creep?

options.text: The size of the change
Whether it was assessed, decided and reflected in the baseline or backlog
Whether the sponsor requested it
Whether it affects the critical path

questions.rationale: Valid change is routed through control; creep is change slipped in silently.

option_rationales.a: Small changes bypassing the process are still creep.
option_rationales.b: Valid change is routed through control; creep is change slipped in silently.
option_rationales.c: A sponsor request still requires assessment and a decision.
option_rationales.d: Schedule impact is one input to the assessment, not the distinction.

questions.prompt: Which is a properly formed definition of done?

options.text: 'The feature is finished'
'The team is satisfied with the result'
'Works on target devices AND passes agreed tests AND meets accessibility criteria'
'The developer has committed the code'

questions.rationale: A definition of done is specific, testable and agreed, so 'done' is not an opinion.

option_rationales.a: 'Finished' is an opinion, not a criterion.
option_rationales.b: Team satisfaction is subjective and untestable.
option_rationales.c: A definition of done is specific, testable and agreed, so 'done' is not an opinion.
option_rationales.d: A commit says nothing about tests or acceptance.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder's request cannot fit the current release. The BEST response is:

options.text: 'No, the scope is frozen.'
'Yes, we will squeeze it in.'
'Please raise it with the sponsor.'
'It is in the backlog at position 6; to pull it in we would move X out — shall we make that trade?'

questions.rationale: Making the trade-off visible protects capacity without becoming the blocker.

option_rationales.a: A flat refusal makes the project manager the obstacle and hides the trade-off.
option_rationales.b: Squeezing it in silently overloads the team and repeats the creep problem.
option_rationales.c: Passing it to the sponsor avoids the conversation the PM should lead.
option_rationales.d: Making the trade-off visible protects capacity without becoming the blocker.

questions.prompt: The critical path is:

options.text: The longest path through the network, determining the shortest possible project duration
The shortest path through the network
The path containing the most expensive activities
The sequence of milestones agreed with the sponsor

questions.rationale: The longest path sets the earliest possible finish; its activities have zero float.

option_rationales.a: The longest path sets the earliest possible finish; its activities have zero float.
option_rationales.b: The shortest path places no constraint on the finish date.
option_rationales.c: Cost has no bearing on which path is critical.
option_rationales.d: Milestones are agreed markers, not a computed path.

questions.prompt: Float (slack) is:

options.text: The buffer added to every estimate
The time a task may slip without delaying the project end
The difference between planned and actual cost
The contingency reserve for schedule risk

questions.rationale: Float is the slack an activity has before it would push the finish date.

option_rationales.a: Buffers are added deliberately; float is a property of the network.
option_rationales.b: Float is the slack an activity has before it would push the finish date.
option_rationales.c: That is cost variance.
option_rationales.d: Reserves are budget provisions, not schedule slack.

questions.prompt: A non-critical activity with 5 days of float slips by 3 days. The project end date will:

options.text: Slip by 3 days
Slip by 5 days
Not change
Improve by 2 days

questions.rationale: A slip within available float does not affect the project finish.

option_rationales.a: A 3-day slip is absorbed by 5 days of float.
option_rationales.b: The activity is not on the critical path, so no such delay occurs.
option_rationales.c: A slip within available float does not affect the project finish.
option_rationales.d: Using float does not shorten the project.

questions.prompt: Crashing a schedule means:

options.text: Running activities in parallel that were sequential
Extending the working day for the whole team
Reducing scope to save time
Adding resources to critical activities, increasing cost

questions.rationale: Crashing buys time with money; fast-tracking buys time with risk.

option_rationales.a: That describes fast-tracking.
option_rationales.b: Longer days may be part of crashing but do not define it.
option_rationales.c: Reducing scope is descoping, not crashing.
option_rationales.d: Crashing buys time with money; fast-tracking buys time with risk.

questions.prompt: Fast-tracking a schedule means:

options.text: Running activities in parallel that were planned sequentially, increasing risk and possible rework
Adding resources to critical activities
Removing quality checks
Negotiating a later deadline

questions.rationale: Overlapping activities adds risk of rework rather than cost.

option_rationales.a: Overlapping activities adds risk of rework rather than cost.
option_rationales.b: That describes crashing.
option_rationales.c: Removing quality checks is not a recognised compression technique.
option_rationales.d: Renegotiating the deadline avoids compression altogether.

questions.prompt: To shorten the project, compression should be applied to:

options.text: The activities with the largest budget
Activities on the critical path only
Activities with the most float
Every activity proportionally

questions.rationale: Compressing non-critical activities saves nothing — a classic exam trap.

option_rationales.a: Budget size does not determine the finish date.
option_rationales.b: Compressing non-critical activities saves nothing — a classic exam trap.
option_rationales.c: Activities with float do not drive the end date.
option_rationales.d: Proportional compression wastes money on non-critical work.

questions.prompt: After successfully compressing the critical path, what MUST the project manager do?

options.text: Re-baseline the budget automatically
Inform the CCB that no further changes are possible
Recompute the network, because a near-critical path may now be longest
Remove float from all remaining activities

questions.rationale: Compression can shift the critical path to another route; always recheck.

option_rationales.a: The budget may change, but the network must be rechecked first.
option_rationales.b: Further changes are always possible through change control.
option_rationales.c: Compression can shift the critical path to another route; always recheck.
option_rationales.d: Float is a computed property, not something you delete.

questions.prompt: Story points in agile estimation represent:

options.text: Hours of effort
The number of team members required
Euros of cost
Relative size and complexity compared with a reference item

questions.rationale: Points are relative sizes, deliberately avoiding false precision in hours.

option_rationales.a: Points deliberately avoid the false precision of hours.
option_rationales.b: Team size is a capacity question, not a size estimate.
option_rationales.c: Cost is derived separately from effort and rates.
option_rationales.d: Points are relative sizes, deliberately avoiding false precision in hours.

questions.prompt: Velocity is best used to:

options.text: Forecast empirically how much backlog fits into future iterations
Commit contractually to a fixed delivery date
Compare the productivity of different teams
Set individual performance targets

questions.rationale: Velocity is an empirical forecasting aid, not a promise or a benchmark between teams.

option_rationales.a: Velocity is an empirical forecasting aid, not a promise or a benchmark between teams.
option_rationales.b: Velocity forecasts probabilistically; it is not a contractual promise.
option_rationales.c: Points are team-specific, so cross-team comparison is meaningless.
option_rationales.d: Individual targets undermine collective ownership.

questions.prompt: Planned Value (PV) is:

options.text: The money actually spent so far
The budgeted cost of the work planned to be done by now
The budgeted cost of the work actually completed
The forecast final cost of the project

questions.rationale: PV is the authorised budget for the scheduled work at a point in time.

option_rationales.a: That is actual cost.
option_rationales.b: PV is the authorised budget for the scheduled work at a point in time.
option_rationales.c: That is earned value.
option_rationales.d: That is estimate at completion.

questions.prompt: Earned Value (EV) is:

options.text: The money actually spent
The remaining budget
The budgeted cost of the work actually completed
The value the customer places on the product

questions.rationale: EV expresses completed work in budget terms — the heart of EVM.

option_rationales.a: That is actual cost.
option_rationales.b: Remaining budget is BAC minus EV, a derived figure.
option_rationales.c: EV expresses completed work in budget terms — the heart of EVM.
option_rationales.d: Customer perception is not an earned-value measure.

questions.prompt: Actual Cost (AC) is:

options.text: The budget at completion
The cost forecast for remaining work
The cost of the original estimate
The cost actually incurred for the work performed

questions.rationale: AC is real expenditure for the work that has been done.

option_rationales.a: BAC is the total authorised budget.
option_rationales.b: That is the estimate to complete.
option_rationales.c: The original estimate is a plan, not an actual.
option_rationales.d: AC is real expenditure for the work that has been done.

questions.prompt: Cost Variance is calculated as:

options.text: EV − AC
PV − AC
EV − PV
BAC − AC

questions.rationale: CV = EV − AC; a negative value means over budget.

option_rationales.a: CV = EV − AC; a negative value means over budget.
option_rationales.b: PV minus AC mixes plan with spend and measures nothing useful.
option_rationales.c: That is schedule variance.
option_rationales.d: BAC minus AC is the remaining budget, not a variance.

questions.prompt: Schedule Variance is calculated as:

options.text: EV − AC
EV − PV
PV − AC
BAC − EV

questions.rationale: SV = EV − PV; a negative value means behind schedule.

option_rationales.a: That is cost variance.
option_rationales.b: SV = EV − PV; a negative value means behind schedule.
option_rationales.c: That mixes plan and actual cost.
option_rationales.d: BAC minus EV is the remaining work in budget terms.

questions.prompt: A project reports CPI = 0.85. This means the project is:

options.text: Under budget
Ahead of schedule
Over budget
Exactly on plan

questions.rationale: CPI = EV/AC; below 1.0 means you get less than one unit of value per unit spent.

option_rationales.a: Under budget would require CPI above 1.0.
option_rationales.b: CPI says nothing about schedule.
option_rationales.c: CPI = EV/AC; below 1.0 means you get less than one unit of value per unit spent.
option_rationales.d: On plan would be exactly 1.0.

questions.prompt: A project reports SPI = 1.10. This means the project is:

options.text: Behind schedule
Under budget
Over budget
Ahead of schedule

questions.rationale: SPI = EV/PV; above 1.0 means more work completed than planned.

option_rationales.a: Behind schedule would require SPI below 1.0.
option_rationales.b: SPI says nothing about budget.
option_rationales.c: SPI measures schedule, not cost.
option_rationales.d: SPI = EV/PV; above 1.0 means more work completed than planned.

questions.prompt: BAC = EUR 200,000 and CPI = 0.90. Using EAC = BAC ÷ CPI, the forecast final cost is approximately:
questions.rationale: 200,000 ÷ 0.90 ≈ 222,000 — about 11% over budget if the trend holds.

option_rationales.a: That would imply CPI above 1.0.
option_rationales.b: That would imply CPI of exactly 1.0.
option_rationales.c: 200,000 ÷ 0.90 ≈ 222,000 — about 11% over budget if the trend holds.
option_rationales.d: That implies a CPI of about 0.83, not 0.90.

questions.prompt: PV = 120k, EV = 90k, AC = 100k. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Schedule performance (SPI 0.75) is worse than cost performance (CPI 0.90)
Cost performance (CPI 0.90) is worse than schedule performance (SPI 0.75)
The project is ahead of schedule and under budget
The project is exactly on plan

questions.rationale: CPI = 0.90 and SPI = 0.75, so the schedule problem is the more severe one.

option_rationales.a: CPI = 0.90 and SPI = 0.75, so the schedule problem is the more severe one.
option_rationales.b: CPI 0.90 is better than SPI 0.75, so cost is the lesser problem.
option_rationales.c: Both indices are below 1.0, so neither is favourable.
option_rationales.d: On plan would require both indices at 1.0.

questions.prompt: Cost of quality reasoning suggests that:

options.text: Inspection at the end is the cheapest control
Prevention and appraisal cost less than internal and external failure
Quality costs cannot be quantified
Failure costs fall as the project progresses

questions.rationale: Preventing a defect is far cheaper than fixing it later, especially after release.

option_rationales.a: End inspection detects defects late, when they are most expensive.
option_rationales.b: Preventing a defect is far cheaper than fixing it later, especially after release.
option_rationales.c: Cost of quality is precisely an attempt to quantify them.
option_rationales.d: Failure costs rise as defects are found later.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between quality and grade?

options.text: They are synonyms
Quality applies to products, grade to services
Grade is the category of features; quality is how well it meets requirements — low grade can be acceptable, low quality never is
Grade is set by the customer, quality by the supplier

questions.rationale: A low-grade product can still be high quality; low quality is always a problem.

option_rationales.a: They are distinct concepts.
option_rationales.b: Both apply to products and services alike.
option_rationales.c: A low-grade product can still be high quality; low quality is always a problem.
option_rationales.d: Grade is a design decision; quality is conformance to requirements.

questions.prompt: Which action embodies prevention rather than inspection?

options.text: Adding a final acceptance test
Increasing the sample size in end-of-line checks
Hiring an external auditor for the closing phase
Validating an early prototype with users and peer-reviewing before merge

questions.rationale: Prevention builds quality in during the work rather than detecting defects afterwards.

option_rationales.a: A final test detects rather than prevents.
option_rationales.b: A larger sample is still inspection.
option_rationales.c: An audit at closing is the latest possible detection.
option_rationales.d: Prevention builds quality in during the work rather than detecting defects afterwards.

questions.prompt: A risk was correctly identified but never actively addressed, and it has now occurred. What was missing?

options.text: Implementation and monitoring of the planned response
Risk identification
The risk register
Stakeholder analysis

questions.rationale: Planning risk is worthless without executing responses and monitoring triggers.

option_rationales.a: Planning risk is worthless without executing responses and monitoring triggers.
option_rationales.b: The risk was correctly identified, so identification was not the gap.
option_rationales.c: A register existed; it simply was not acted upon.
option_rationales.d: Stakeholder analysis is unrelated to executing a response.

questions.prompt: A secondary risk is:

options.text: A low-priority risk
A risk that arises directly from implementing a risk response
A risk affecting a supplier rather than the project
A risk that has already occurred

questions.rationale: Responses can create new risks, which must themselves be managed.

option_rationales.a: Priority does not define a secondary risk.
option_rationales.b: Responses can create new risks, which must themselves be managed.
option_rationales.c: Ownership of the risk does not make it secondary.
option_rationales.d: An occurred risk is an issue.

questions.prompt: A fixed-price contract places most risk on the:

options.text: Buyer
End user
Seller
Regulator

questions.rationale: Fixed price shifts scope and cost risk to the seller — but only works with clear scope.

option_rationales.a: The buyer carries more risk under cost-reimbursable arrangements.
option_rationales.b: End users are not parties to the contract.
option_rationales.c: Fixed price shifts scope and cost risk to the seller — but only works with clear scope.
option_rationales.d: Regulators set rules; they do not bear contractual risk.

questions.prompt: Which contract type best suits research and development work with uncertain scope?

options.text: Firm fixed price
Fixed-price economic price adjustment
Fixed price with incentive fee only
Cost-reimbursable

questions.rationale: With undefined scope, cost-reimbursable is appropriate and the buyer carries more risk.

option_rationales.a: Firm fixed price on unknown scope guarantees change-order conflict.

questions.rationale: Prevention and appraisal are investments; internal and external failure are the costs they avoid. External failure — a defect reaching the customer — is by far the most expensive, which is why prevention beats inspection.

questions.rationale: Accept, transition, learn, recognise, hand over the benefit. Value leaks at every skipped step — most often at lessons learned and benefit hand-over.
